bullets: The newly released Spec-Test Coverage Gap study audits whether coding-agent tests enforce requirements absent from the task description. It introduces a four-point overspecification scale and flags a task when two language-model judges independently score the gap at three or above. A separate new errata dataset records the same defect class alongside grader bugs and leaked reference programs, making benchmark validity a recurring pressure in this captured feed rather than a one-off concern. Why it matters: If you are choosing or maintaining a coding-agent suite, this provides a concrete pre-ranking audit: separate failures caused by the agent from failures caused by hidden grader expectations. That can change which tasks remain eligible and whether model rankings are defensible. Evidence: E007, E056. High confidence.

ICLWorld is a newly released online benchmark for in-context learning, meaning an agent must infer new rules from demonstrations supplied during use rather than from additional training. It evaluates the same adaptation capability across computer and robot tasks through UIverse, a harness that presents every environment as a user interface, and includes 30 environments. Why it matters: If you are selecting an agent evaluation for adaptation, ICLWorld offers a single protocol across digital and physical operation instead of relying on static text or image tests. This lets teams test whether adaptation transfers between interfaces and embodied tasks without equating offline accuracy with interactive performance. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

RecurSciBench is a newly released benchmark for recursive self-improvement, where a scientific agent uses experience from earlier work to improve later work. Its RecurSciPipe framework constructs modeling and data-analysis tasks from raw datasets and checks outputs through execution and scientific-validity tests. Why it matters: If you are evaluating research agents, this changes the target from completing isolated questions to measuring whether improvements transfer across executable scientific tasks. Independent verification also gives product and research teams a basis for distinguishing genuine task gains from an agent merely claiming that it improved. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

RoboProbe is a newly released benchmark for checking whether robot world models generate physically plausible videos. Rather than using only broad semantic judgments, it defines five metrics tied to physical laws and combines spatial and temporal evidence to identify implausible interactions. Why it matters: If generated video informs robot planning, visual realism alone does not establish that an action is feasible. RoboProbe offers a way to compare world models on specific physical violations before their simulated outcomes are used to propose or reject real-world actions. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

INCLUDE-2.0 is a newly released multilingual factual benchmark that separates language proficiency from regional knowledge. It contains more than 220,000 samples covering 91 languages, 86 countries, and 127 language-country pairs, with question types that distinguish context-independent facts from answers that vary by country or community. Why it matters: If you are evaluating a multilingual assistant, an aggregate score can hide whether failures come from understanding the language or lacking the relevant regional knowledge. INCLUDE-2.0 supports separate product decisions about language support and country-specific factual coverage. Evidence: E021. High confidence.

FigmaEval is a newly released benchmark for agents operating professional user-interface design software. Its 84 tasks and 783 screens use constrained specifications but allow multiple valid solutions, leaving agents to choose layouts, visual hierarchy, components, and presentation rather than reproduce one fixed reference. Why it matters: If you are choosing a suite for design agents, this tests compliance with requirements without treating open-ended design as exact image matching. It therefore targets the decision an agent actually makes—how to satisfy a brief—while preserving standardized task inputs for comparison. Evidence: E009. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 Spec-Test Coverage Gap 研究审查编码智能体测试是否强制执行任务描述中未包含的要求。该研究提出了一个四级过度规范量表，并在两个语言模型评审者各自独立地将差距评为三级或以上时标记该任务。另一个新发布的勘误数据集记录了同一类缺陷，以及评分器错误和泄露的参考程序，这使基准有效性成为此次采集信息流中反复出现的压力，而非一次性问题。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择或维护编码智能体评测套件，这提供了一项具体的排名前审查：将智能体导致的失败与评分器隐藏预期导致的失败区分开来。这可能改变哪些任务仍具备纳入资格，以及模型排名是否站得住脚。Evidence: E007, E056. High confidence.

ICLWorld 是一个新发布的在线上下文学习基准，这意味着智能体必须从使用期间提供的示例中推断新规则，而不是通过额外训练学习。它通过 UIverse 在计算机和机器人任务中评估相同的适应能力；该测试框架将每个环境都呈现为用户界面，并包含 30 个环境。Why it matters: 如果你正在为适应能力选择智能体评测，ICLWorld 提供了一套横跨数字与物理操作的统一协议，而非依赖静态文本或图像测试。这让团队能够测试适应能力是否可在不同界面与具身任务之间迁移，同时避免将离线准确率等同于交互性能。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

RecurSciBench 是一个新发布的递归自我改进基准，其中科学智能体利用先前工作的经验改进后续工作。其 RecurSciPipe 框架基于原始数据集构建建模与数据分析任务，并通过执行测试和科学有效性测试来检查输出。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估科研智能体，这会将目标从完成孤立问题转变为衡量改进能否迁移到可执行的科学任务中。独立验证也为产品和研究团队提供了依据，使其能够区分真实的任务增益与智能体仅仅声称自己有所改进。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

RoboProbe 是一个新发布的基准，用于检验机器人世界模型生成的视频在物理上是否合理。它没有仅使用宽泛的语义判断，而是定义了五项与物理定律相关的指标，并结合空间和时间证据来识别不合理的交互。Why it matters: 如果生成的视频用于机器人规划，仅凭视觉逼真度并不能证明某个动作可行。RoboProbe 提供了一种方法，可在世界模型的模拟结果被用于提出或否决现实世界动作之前，根据具体的物理违规情况比较这些模型。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

INCLUDE-2.0 是一个新发布的多语言事实性基准，将语言熟练度与区域知识区分开来。它包含超过 220,000 个样本，覆盖 91 种语言、86 个国家和 127 个语言—国家组合，其问题类型可区分不依赖语境的事实与因国家或社群而异的答案。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估多语言助手，汇总分数可能会掩盖失败究竟源于语言理解不足，还是缺少相关区域知识。INCLUDE-2.0 支持分别就语言支持和特定国家的事实覆盖范围做出产品决策。Evidence: E021. High confidence.

FigmaEval 是一个新发布的基准，用于评估在专业用户界面设计软件中操作的智能体。其 84 项任务和 783 个屏幕采用受约束的规范，但允许多种有效解决方案，让智能体自行选择布局、视觉层级、组件和呈现方式，而不是复现一个固定参考。Why it matters: 如果你正在为设计智能体选择评测套件，该基准测试智能体对要求的遵循情况，同时不会将开放式设计视为精确的图像匹配。因此，它针对的是智能体实际做出的决策——如何满足设计简报——同时保留标准化任务输入以供比较。Evidence: E009. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.
evidence_items.title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are advancing the automation of data-driven scientific research. Recent advances in recursive self-improvement (RSI) offer the potential for these agents to continuously improve through experience, but evaluating transfer across scientific tasks requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment of self-improvement gains. We introduce RecurSciBench, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research. Its RecurSciPipe framework automatically constructs scientific modeling and data analysis tasks from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and scientific validity checks. RecurSciBench spans four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied scientific objectives. We evaluate four RSI systems by comparing their initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. Experiments show that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains. Positive overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks. Experience can transfer across task types and benefit other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.
evidence_items.title: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating the physical plausibility of generated videos is critical for reliable robotic planning with world models. These videos inform action proposal and assessment before real-world execution, so undetected physical violations can lead to erroneous assessments of action feasibility and safety. Yet current video generators often produce physically implausible interactions. Detecting such violations directly with vision-language models (VLMs) remains challenging as physical verification requires evidence-grounded spatiotemporal reasoning beyond high-level semantic understanding. We develop five law-specific metrics for evaluating physical plausibility by combining spatiotemporal evidence from segmentation, tracking, 3D geometry, or appearance comparisons with targeted VLM reasoning: Contact fidelity, Object persistence, Solidity, Robot deformation, and Object deformation. Building on this metric suite, we introduce RoboProbe, an agentic evaluation framework that coordinates metric execution and selectively refines evaluations through constrained actions. To evaluate the physical plausibility of robot world models, we further introduce RP-Bench, with 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations of 239 manipulation tasks from 12 robot datasets. On RP-Bench, all five metrics achieve AUROCs above 0.85 and outperform the evaluated learned judges, prior evaluators, and a frames-only Gemini baseline. Applying these metrics to five video generators reveals distinct patterns of physical violations across models, in both violation types and frequencies.
evidence_items.title: RoboProbe: Benchmarking Physical Plausibility of Robot World Models

evidence_items.summary: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
evidence_items.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Summary. A curated, machine-readable Chinese-language corpus for the Xiaoqinling gold ore field (Shaanxi–Henan, China), built from 153 research articles (1977–2014) retrieved from CNKI (OCR parsing and layout-driven boundary detection expand the 153 articles into 163 article-level records; a complete mapping table, paper id map.csv, links every record to its source article). The release comprises: 7,698 typed text chunks (text 6,314 / table 433 / image 744 / equation 207); 5,886 geological concept cards (5,453 unique per vector-index count) with definitions, aliases, relational links and per-card source provenance; 756 figure objects with VLM-based classification and structured descriptions, of which 283 carry human-verified type annotations; a 191-item three-tier retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) evaluation set (core 90 / coverage 81 / adversarial 20, including refusal, boundary and safety categories) with numeric-interval, citation-strictness and LLM-judge scoring keys; a 153-entry source bibliography covering all 163 article-level records; and the processing scripts.Methods. Full-text PDFs were parsed with MinerU 2.6.8; a purpose-built cleaning pipeline (page-continuation merging, filler-paper removal, header/footer and metadata-line extraction, whitelist-based OCR corrections) ran before chunking. Concepts were extracted with LLM assistance (GLM-4 API; qwen3:8b locally hosted) under a typed schema with rule-based merging and a five-stage quality-improvement pass (sampled clean-card rate 52%→100%; 2,363 corrections in timestamped audit logs). Figures were processed classify-then-describe with qwen2.5vl:7b and targeted human review. Data quality was mapped against Chinese standards GB/T 36344-2018, DZ/T 0268-2014 and GB/T 42381.8-2023, with seven gaps (G1–G7) disclosed.Scope note. evidence_items.summary: Overview This repository contains the research data, computational engine, experimental records, statistical analysis scripts, and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript entitled “A standards-aware AI copilot architecture for highway geometric-design quality assurance,” under revision for the ASCE Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering (Manuscript ID: CPENG-8885). The research proposes a hybrid deterministic-generative expert system for highway geometric-design quality assurance (HID-QA), separating deterministic compliance calculations, grounded large language model (LLM) explanations, and workflow-based decision routing while retaining professional engineering decision authority with qualified engineers. Version 2.0 — Research Extensions Version 2.0 extends the original repository (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22044826) by incorporating additional prospective experiments, independent computational verification, corridor-clustered statistical analyses, and expanded methodological and engineering qualification documentation. The original historical experimental evidence, computational engine, benchmark geometries, and encoded reference classifications are preserved. Repository Contents HID-QA-50 benchmark comprising 50 constructed highway corridors. Eight encoded geometric-design checks, producing 400 check-level reference classifications. Frozen deterministic computational engine and encoded engineering criteria. Archived August 2026 Grok 4.6 experimental prompts and completions. One hundred prospective agent sessions conducted in November 2026 under two different computational information-access configurations. Prospective model completions and sanitized native request-level execution records. Historical and prospective scoring scripts. Corridor-clustered statistical analyses and confidence interval calculations. Independent computational recoding of the eight geometric-design checks.
evidence_items.title: A Standards-Aware AI Copilot Architecture for Highway Geometric-Design Quality Assurance: HID-QA-50 Dataset, Computational Engine, Agent Evaluation, and Reproducibility Package

evidence_items.summary: This repository accompanies the manuscript entitled “Reflection Interference, Cross-Dataset Generalisation and Spatial-Support Constraints in Automated Pupil Localisation: An Empirical and Mathematical Benchmark”. The study comprises six experimental phases examining reflection restoration, resolution-dependent detection, multiscale geometric estimation, supervised coordinate regression, participant-separated evaluation, cross-dataset generalisation and spatial-support constraints using the MRL Eye Dataset and Labelled Pupils in the Wild (LPW). The repository contains research notebooks, a numerical replication script, 28 aggregate experimental tables, mathematical analysis results, numerical figures, software environment documentation, a data dictionary and reproducibility documentation. Numerical replication using privately retained prediction records successfully reproduced all nine final scientific tables and passed 17 principal numerical checks across 249,626 prediction records. No discrepancies were reported in recalculated localisation errors, detection-validity indicators, threshold-based accuracy or geometric lower-bound verification. The public archive excludes raw eye images, videos, frame-level prediction records and trained models pending confirmation of their redistribution conditions. Consequently, complete prediction-level numerical replication requires access to the corresponding research records. The investigation characterises pupil-localisation performance and failure mechanisms. It does not establish clinical diagnostic performance or claim superiority over state-of-the-art pupil detectors.
evidence_items.title: Replication Package: Reflection Interference, Cross-Dataset Generalisation and Spatial-Support Constraints in Automated Pupil Localisation: An Empirical and Mathematical Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each issue. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.
evidence_items.title: Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in AI agents have enabled autonomous UI design using professional tools such as Figma, yet evaluating their design capabilities remains challenging due to the open-ended nature of design tasks and the absence of unique ground truths. We introduce FigmaEval, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on professional UI design tasks, comprising 84 tasks and 783 screens derived from real-world Figma design files. FigmaEval adopts a constrained-specification, open-solution paradigm, standardizing task requirements and design resources while allowing agents to independently determine layouts, visual hierarchies, component composition, and visual presentation. To assess design quality beyond reference similarity, we develop 22 expert-grounded evaluation rubrics across six dimensions and introduce a human evaluation arena where professional designers compare agent-generated designs through blinded pairwise judgments. Evaluating eleven models under a unified Figma agent setup, we find substantial agreement between rubric-based assessments and human preferences, alongside distinct differences in design practices and quality--efficiency trade-offs. FigmaEval provides a framework for systematically assessing professional UI design capabilities and understanding the strengths and limitations of current AI agents.
evidence_items.title: FigmaEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents in Professional UI Design

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.
evidence_items.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?

evidence_items.summary: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.
evidence_items.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion

evidence_items.summary: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.
evidence_items.title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action

evidence_items.summary: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
evidence_items.title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?

evidence_items.summary: Low-resource languages remain underrepresented in ASR benchmarks, limiting the ability to reliably assess and compare model performance. We present a large-scale benchmark for automatic speech recognition (ASR) on low-resource languages in Africa. The benchmark harmonizes six public corpora into a unified, reproducible evaluation framework and evaluates 52 state-of-the-art ASR models spanning three model architectural paradigms across 39 African languages on diverse datasets. Models are evaluated using standard accuracy and efficiency metrics, word error rate (WER), character error rate (CER), and inverse real-time factor (RTFx). This benchmark introduces architecture-aware comparison that systematically analyzes both individual models and broader model families. In addition, we quantify linguistic variance across language families, revealing how these factors shape ASR performance across diverse African languages. We also provide a comprehensive accuracy and efficiency trade-off analysis directly relevant to deployment in low-resource settings. Together, the benchmark, evaluation pipeline, and results support transparent, reproducible, and deployment-aware evaluation of ASR models for low-resource languages.
evidence_items.title: PazaBench: Large-Scale ASR Benchmark for Low-Resource Languages in Africa

evidence_items.summary: Current multilingual benchmarks cover only a fraction of the languages represented in modern pretraining corpora and often conflate language proficiency with the ability to answer questions grounded in specific regions and communities. We introduce INCLUDE-2.0, a large-scale benchmark for region-aware multilingual factual evaluation, which covers 91 languages from 86 countries (127 total language--country pairs), comprising over 220K curated samples drawn from native regional sources. Unlike existing benchmarks that often treat language as a proxy for region, IINCLUDE-2.0 distinguishes between questions whose answers are independent of context, vary by country, concern widely documented facts about a place, or depend on knowledge primarily expressed through local linguistic and cultural sources. Each item is annotated with its regional knowledge type and domain, and paired with an English translation, enabling controlled analysis of the relationship between language proficiency and possession of regional knowledge. Evaluating frontier and open-weight models on IINCLUDE-2.0, we find that aggregate multilingual accuracy masks substantial variation across regional knowledge types, languages, and regions. We find that frontier models perform worse on locally embedded knowledge than on widely documented facts about regions, with an average drop of ~14.5 points. We also show that for open-weight models, scale improves accuracy but does not reliably make performance invariant to whether a question is asked in English or its original language. INCLUDE-2.0 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/epfl-nlp/include-2.0
evidence_items.title: INCLUDE-2.0: Disentangling Knowledge Gaps in Multilingual LLM Evaluation

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.
evidence_items.title: HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots

evidence_items.summary: Widely used spatial-QA benchmarks increasingly motivate embodied navigation, yet evaluate foundation vision-language models (VLMs) through isolated queries about space rather than feasible action sequences in space. However, zero-shot waypoint navigation requires turning spatial understanding into a feasible action sequence: from a single first-person view, a model must jointly ground the target, respect agent-specific clearance, maintain edge-by-edge legality, and stop at the goal. To evaluate this capability, we introduce EgoPathBench, a dataset and five-task benchmark for first-person waypoint decision-making. Each example pairs an egocentric RGB image, a natural-language goal, and numbered visible waypoints, and scores predicted candidate sets or ordered routes against registered 3D scene geometry under task-specific Point or Embodied feasibility graphs. EgoPathBench comprises 31,852 training, 1,345 validation, and 1,111 benchmark questions, with at least one verified reference route for every route question. Across ten foundation VLMs, the highest EgoPath Score is only 35.6. While models often make locally plausible choices and the top model reaches 41.7% success on Point Path, it drops to 10.0% on both Embodied Path and Intent Path, with the remaining nine models below 3% on Embodied Path (and at most 4.0% on Intent Path) -- exposing a sharp gap between local plausibility and complete embodied routes. Beyond evaluation, we construct the EgoPath-SFT training set. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-4B on EgoPath-SFT raises its EgoPath Score from 3.9 to 38.9, improves closed-loop Isaac Sim execution by 20 percentage points, and transfers consistently to three external spatial benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: EgoPathBench: Evaluating Zero-Shot Egocentric Waypoint Decision-Making in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multi-frame video frame interpolation (VFI) aims to reconstruct dense video from sparse keyframes, requiring accurate intermediate motion and faithful appearance. As temporal gaps grow, flow-based methods can retain observed textures but misplace them under ambiguous motion, whereas iterative latent-diffusion models can synthesize plausible content but incur substantial sampling costs and may alter details during reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE). We present RePix-VFI, named for Re-rendering observed Pixels, a multi-frame VFI framework that couples draft-conditioned one-step video diffusion with reconstruction from observed keyframes. A pretrained video diffusion model refines a flow-rendered draft of the whole window in a single forward pass. For each target frame, our generative readback matches its two bounding keyframes to the generated prediction using an optical-flow estimator. The resulting correspondences guide re-rendering of original keyframe RGB pixels outside the VAE. A lightweight appearance fusion head combines these renderings with generated appearance. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction and perceptual quality. On SNU-FILM at $\times$8 and $\times$16, RePix-VFI achieves the highest PSNR and the lowest LPIPS, FloLPIPS, and tOF among the compared methods, exceeding the best evaluated diffusion-based baseline by 1.71 and 1.48dB in PSNR, respectively. It also runs 32--42$\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art multi-frame VFI diffusion model.
evidence_items.title: RePix-VFI: Re-rendering Observed Pixels for Video Frame Interpolation with Generative Priors from One-Step Diffusion

evidence_items.summary: Spectral imaging captures information that ordinary RGB sensors cannot, but dedicated spectral cameras can be expensive and bulky. Recovering dense spectra from RGB images offers an accessible alternative, but distinct spectra can produce the same camera response, generating an ambiguity that even more advanced recovery algorithms cannot always resolve. Therefore, increasing the spectral information captured at acquisition is essential. We propose DualSpec, a stereo acquisition framework that jointly optimizes two external optical filters and a reconstruction network. Each filter is placed in front of a standard RGB camera, and the two are designed to produce six responses that provide complementary information for the network. Experiments across reconstruction architectures and spectral ranges show that DualSpec reduces mean spectral angle error by 36-72% relative to a single RGB camera and by 11-29% relative to stereo pairs selected from commercial filters. Cross-dataset evaluations, including a new benchmark of spectral images captured from displaced viewpoints, show that the method generalizes and remains robust to viewpoint misalignment, while analyses of thin-film approximations support optical feasibility.
evidence_items.title: DualSpec: Spectral Reconstruction with Optimized Stereo Cameras

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.
evidence_items.title: MRBench: Benchmarking Physical Necessity Reasoning in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.
evidence_items.title: A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in vision-language foundation models have enabled open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) without task-specific training, offering new opportunities for Earth Observation (EO) applications. However, their capabilities for cloud detection remain insufficiently explored. In this work, we evaluate twelve OVSS approaches across six publicly available EO datasets in a zero-shot setting, i.e., without fine-tuning or adaptation to the target data. We investigate both binary cloud detection and multiclass segmentation, distinguishing between thick clouds, thin clouds, cloud shadows, and background. Our results show differences in performance across models and datasets, with SegEarth-OV3 achieving the highest binary cloud detection performance on four of the six datasets. While several approaches demonstrate promising performance in binary cloud detection, multiclass segmentation remains more challenging, particularly when distinguishing between fine-grained cloud categories. Furthermore, our controlled prompt sensitivity analysis reveals model-dependent responses to alternative textual descriptions, with appearance-oriented prompts benefiting certain approaches while degrading the performance of others. Overall, our findings demonstrate both the potential and current limitations of zero-shot OVSS for cloud detection, establishing a comparative benchmark for future research on generalisable cloud segmentation. Code will be available at: https://github.com/josesosajs/zero-shot-cloudovss.
evidence_items.title: On the Capabilities and Limitations of Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Cloud Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).
evidence_items.title: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.
evidence_items.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Verifying image authenticity is a critical need for a variety of applications and decision-making in the remote sensing (RS) domain, yet it is becoming more challenging as advancements in generative AI enable producing increasingly realistic synthetic overhead data. However, existing RS deepfake benchmarks prioritize sheer volume at the expense of visual realism and diversity, while also lacking rigorous out-of-distribution (OOD) testing protocols to evaluate real-world robustness. To address this, we introduce the Geospatial Deepfakes Dataset (GDD), a benchmark for RS deepfake detection and manipulation localization. Rather than relying on uncurated, redundant synthetic generation, GDD comprises images across diverse modern generative models and real image sources, alongside manipulations from diffusion inpainting, splicing, and copy-move operations. Crucially, GDD establishes an OOD evaluation protocol for deepfake detection comprising unseen real image sources and generative models. We benchmark five deepfake detectors and two localization models across intra- and cross-dataset regimes and reveal that detectors trained on high-volume, uncurated benchmarks overfit to dataset-specific artifacts, whereas training on GDD yields superior cross-dataset generalization despite its compact scale. This benchmarking also exposes critical failure modes in current state-of-the-art methods. Combined, GDD and its evaluation protocol establish a high-quality standard for developing and stress-testing detection and localization models in this safety-critical RS domain. The dataset is publicly available.
evidence_items.title: GDD: A Remote Sensing Image Deepfake Detection and Manipulation Localization Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in MLLMs have improved social understanding, enabling models to recognize emotions and distinguish truthful from deceptive behaviors. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on coarse-grained emotion recognition or binary truth-deception detection, overlooking the diverse ways people manipulate information in conversations, such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. Understanding these behaviors requires reasoning about underlying facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context, making them difficult to evaluate reliably. To address this gap, we introduce InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. InfoCon identifies six fine-grained strategies and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. We develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to construct and verify reliable labels from rich contextual evidence. We benchmark representative multimodal models and systematically analyze their fine-grained information manipulation understanding, providing a testbed beyond binary truth-deception judgments.
evidence_items.title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations

evidence_items.summary: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
evidence_items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake

evidence_items.summary: Existing voice AI assistants treat every detected pause as an invitation to speak. This works in dyadic dialogue, but in multi-party settings, where an AI assistant participates alongside multiple speakers, pauses are abundant and ambiguous. An assistant that speaks on every pause becomes disruptive rather than useful. In this work, we formulate context-aware turn-taking: at every detected pause, given the full conversation context, our method decides whether the assistant should speak or stay silent. We introduce a benchmark of over 120K labeled conversations spanning three multi-party corpora. Evaluating eight recent large language models, we find that they consistently fail at context-aware turn-taking under zero-shot prompting. We then propose a supervised fine-tuning approach with reasoning traces, improving balanced accuracy by up to 23 percentage points. Our findings suggest that context-aware turn-taking is not an emergent capability; it must be explicitly trained.
evidence_items.title: Speak or Stay Silent: Context-Aware Turn-Taking in Multi-Party Dialogue

evidence_items.summary: Federated Learning (FL) is a widespread and well-adopted paradigm of decentralised learning that allows training one model from multiple sources without the need to transfer data between participating clients directly. Since its inception in 2016, it has been divided into numerous subfields that deal with application-specific issues, such as data heterogeneity or resource allocation. One such sub-field, Clustered Federated Learning (CFL), is dealing with the problem of clustering the population of clients into separate cohorts to deliver personalised models. Although a few remarkable works have been published in this domain, the problem remains largely unexplored, as its basic assumptions and settings differ slightly from those of standard FL. In this work, we present One-Shot Clustered Federated Learning (OCFL), a clustering-agnostic algorithm that can automatically detect the earliest suitable moment for clustering. We empirically evaluate our methodology by testing various one-shot clustering algorithms for over forty different tasks on five benchmark datasets. Our experiments showcase the good performance of our approach when used to perform CFL in an automated manner without the need to adjust hyperparameters. We also revisit the practical feasibility of CFL algorithms based on the gradients or weights of the clients, providing firm evidence of the high efficiency of density-based clustering methods when used to differentiate between the loss surfaces of neural networks trained on different distributions. Moreover, by inspecting the feasibility of local explanations generated with the help of GradCAM, we can provide more insights into the relationship between personalisation and the explainability of local predictions.
evidence_items.title: One-Shot Clustering for Federated Learning Under Clustering-Agnostic Assumption

evidence_items.summary: Gradient-flux (GF) approaches present an important chance to expand ecosystem-atmosphere observations beyond the gases routinely measured using eddy covariance (EC) alone. We developed a dataset to explore when and where gradient-flux approaches work across diverse ecosystems. We utilized standardized observations from 47 terrestrial sites within the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) to develop this continental benchmark dataset for evaluating the performance of three GF approaches, the modified Bowen ratio (MBR), aerodynamic (AE), and wind-profile (WP) methods, against co-located EC measurements of CO2 and H2O. This multi-site benchmark dataset comprises EC and GF fluxes by method and sampling height pair, along with corresponding micrometeorological data. Additional data include: storage fluxes, gradient-flux ensembles, site-level canopy complexity and metadata for tower geometry and sensor heights, ustar thresholds, metadata for validation sites, site canopy attributes, site concentration profiles, and site sampling height pairs.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark dataset for comparing eddy covariance measurements and gradient flux calculations across 47 National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) flux towers, August 2021 - August 2026

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the supplementary materials and experimental data supporting the research article "Conversational Retrieval of System Dynamics Models by Feedback Structure Using Signed Causal Graphs". The corpus of 63 System Dynamics models is published separately (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18047724), and the 37 topical scenarios of Set 1 with their relevance judgments are part of the dataset of the previous study (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22164313). The dataset is divided into four components: the structural query set (Set 2), the aggregated run outputs, the per-block checkpoints, and the run manifest. 1. Structural Query Set (Set 2) File graphrag-set2.csv: The 40 structural scenarios. Each row contains the scenario number, the domain, three phrasings of the same request (a broad intent, a refinement and an expert query) and the identifiers of the relevant models (GoldenUuids). Scenarios with the domain Theory are structural requests without a topical anchor (scenarios 19, 20, 23 to 29, 32 and 35). File graphrag-set2-goldspec.jsonl: The gold structural specification of each scenario, one JSON object per line. A specification can contain loop constraints (polarity R or B, involves terms, minimum length), constraints on archetype, behaviour mode, external forcing and model size, a strength (must or should) for each constraint, and curated synonym lists for the involves terms. The relevant models in graphrag-set2.csv were computed from these specifications by the independent oracle. File set2-archetype-scenarios.txt: The scenarios that carry an archetype constraint (21, 22 and 23), used for the descriptive comparison of H with H-noarch. 2. Aggregated Run Outputs All runs used .NET 10.0 on Windows 11 (AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 7840U, CPU only), with five sampling seeds (42, 7, 123, 1234 and 2026), giving 120 blocks and 4,620 scenario executions. All CSV files are semicolon-delimited and UTF-8 encoded. Numeric values use a decimal point.

evidence_items.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems perform strongly on native-English benchmarks, yet their accuracy degrades sharply when the input speech comes from under represented non-native accents. Nepali-accented English is particularly under-served: existing resources either focus on native Nepali speech, cover broader multi-accent settings without dedicated Nepali evaluation, or provide only limited Nepali-accent coverage. This paper presents a Nepali-accented English evaluation dataset designed to support robust ASR benchmarking under accent mismatch. The corpus was collected through a web-based platform that did not collect directly identifying metadata and contains recordings from 57 speakers. Each session follows a fixed 22-prompt protocol consisting of 11 phonetic prompts, 10 domain prompts, and 1 spontaneous prompt, providing complementary coverage of pronunciation, topical vocabulary, and natural speaking style. In addition to transcribed speech, the dataset includes participant metadata for coarse exploratory subgroup analysis and speaker-level manual recording-quality labels. Manual quality assessment shows that 50.9% of sessions are clean and 42.1% contain only mild noise. As a descriptive reference, open-source ASR baselines are substantially worse on this corpus than the corresponding LibriSpeech test-clean values reported in official model cards, reaching 38.15-55.00% WER on the collected set versus reported 2-4% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. These baseline results position the corpus as a practical held-out resource for evaluating accent robustness and out-of-distribution generalization on Nepali-accented English.
evidence_items.title: A Nepali-Accented English Evaluation Dataset for Automatic Speech Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) play a critical role in modern cybersecurity; however, traditional signature- and rule-based approaches remain limited against zero-day, polymorphic, and adaptive cyberattacks. Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) have introduced new opportunities for improving intrusion detection through adaptive learning, synthetic traffic generation, autonomous response, and adversarial robustness. This systematic literature review synthesises evidence from 78 studies published between 2018-2026, providing a comprehensive analysis of the emerging role of Generative AI and Agentic AI in NIDSs. The reviewed studies are organised into four major research themes: (i) data augmentation and synthetic attack generation, (ii) adversarial robustness, (iii) autonomous intrusion detection, and (iv) explainable and trustworthy AI. The analysis shows that generative models, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), diffusion models, and Large Language Models (LLMs), improve synthetic data generation, mitigate class imbalance, and enhance anomaly detection, while agentic approaches based on reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems increase adaptability and distributed decision-making. The review identifies a persistent gap between benchmark performance and operational readiness, driven by limitations in cross-dataset generalisation, computational overhead, adversarial robustness, explainability, privacy preservation, and real-world deployment. To address these challenges, this review proposes a Generative-Agentic Synergy Framework that integrates generative simulation, adaptive detection, agentic response, trust and explainability, and privacy-aware deployment into a unified conceptual framework for designing and evaluating next-generation NIDSs.
evidence_items.title: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence for network intrusion detection: a systematic literature review

evidence_items.summary: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as the de facto learning paradigm for privacy-preserving collaborative model training. Despite its privacy advantages, FL remains vulnerable to backdoor attacks that can compromise global model integrity. In this work, we propose Deployment Activation Backdoor (DAB), a training-assisted, deployment-activated attack that manipulates intermediate feature representations at inference time. DAB uses a single malicious participant to estimate a multiplicative feature perturbation through a one-round calibration procedure, and the learned perturbation is subsequently applied to the deployed global model when a predefined trigger is detected in an input. We investigate this approach in federated models trained via Federated Averaging (FedAvg) under heterogeneous client data distributions generated through Dirichlet partitioning. Although deployment-stage attacks can introduce malicious functionality into already-trained models by altering parameters or inference-time execution, their effectiveness in federated settings—particularly when an adversary accesses only a single client’s local partition—remains insufficiently explored. Our preliminary evaluation shows a substantial drop in the effectiveness of existing deployment-stage attacks when data are restricted to one client’s local partition rather than a centralized dataset, motivating an examination of federated optimization, local data heterogeneity, and inference-time feature manipulation. Evaluating DAB on benchmark image classification datasets in terms of attack success rate and clean classification accuracy, we highlight the importance of assessing deployment-stage backdoor risks under realistic federated conditions where distributed training and limited local data affect inference-time attacks.
evidence_items.title: Deployment Stage Feature Space Backdoor in Federated Learning

evidence_items.summary: Dietary decisions require identifying a food's nutrient content and considering individual dietary needs, but recognizing food from an image alone does not provide this information. Visually similar foods can have different nutrient profiles, so selecting the wrong food record can lead to incorrect decisions even when nutrient rules are applied correctly. Furthermore, satisfying nutrient constraints does not necessarily establish a food's relevance to a person's intake. Evaluating these challenges together requires connecting food images, nutrient records, and individual intake histories. To support this evaluation, we introduce UMAMI (Unified Multimodal Assessment of Meals and Intake), a multimodal dataset and benchmark linking independently collected food images with nutrient profiles and respondent health and intake records. Using this dataset, we construct three diagnostic tasks covering visual nutrient question answering, personalized food recommendation, and condition-aware food substitution. Paired instances and input controls examine how visual identity and respondent context affect decisions. Our experiments identify errors in both food-record selection and nutrient-rule application, while showing that higher rule compliance does not necessarily improve alignment with subsequent recorded intake. These findings highlight the need to evaluate how multimodal systems select and use structured evidence for dietary decisions. The dataset, code, and dashboard are available at https://umami-benchmark.github.io.
evidence_items.title: UMAMI: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Evidence-Grounded Dietary Decisions

evidence_items.summary: Accurate teak-tree segmentation from high-resolution drone imagery is critical for sustainable plantation management, yet lacks dedicated benchmarks. We introduce TeakTreeNet, a comprehensive dataset and evaluation protocol for binary teak-tree segmentation at native 2cm resolution. Four state-of-the-art architectures: U-Net, PSPNet, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer were rigorously benchmarked across scratch and ImageNet-pretrained settings with three-seed reproducibility. SegFormer establishes new SOTA performance with F1 0.938 +/- 0.002 (Teak), IoU 0.968 +/- 0.001 (Teak), and Accuracy 0.986 +/- 0.001, outperforming all pretrained CNNs. Domain-adaptive training suffices, as the scratch SegFormer outperforms ImageNet pretrained baselines, avoiding large-scale pretraining overhead. Comprehensive analysis reveals Transformer's superior boundary delineation for dense plantation scenarios. TeakTreeNet provides researchers with 6391 expertly annotated drone patches (224x224) and establishes reproducible evaluation protocols, enabling direct comparison of future methods. Our benchmark demonstrates SegFormer's optimal balance of accuracy, efficiency, and deployability for operational forestry monitoring of teak plantations for India's western tropical forests.
evidence_items.title: A High-Resolution UAV Benchmark Dataset and Baseline Evaluation for Teak Crown Segmentation in Western Ghats Tropical Forests

evidence_items.summary: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.
evidence_items.title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

evidence_items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24492277. SUMMARY This paper introduces the first publicly released benchmark for evaluating how well accessibility assessment approaches — in this study, five large language models — can judge the accessibility of scholarly PDFs. The authors selected 35 highly cited papers, used Adobe Acrobat Pro to create controlled variants of each, and produced a dataset of 125 PDFs spanning seven WCAG 2.2 / PDF/UA-derived criteria (alternative text quality, semantic tagging, logical reading order, table structure, functional hyperlinks, color contrast, and font readability), each labelled Passed, Failed, Not Present, or Cannot Tell. Labels were checked by one accessibility specialist. Five models (GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o-Vision, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Llama-3.2-Vision-Instruct) were then run zero-shot against criterion-specific extracted inputs, three times each. GPT-4-Turbo achieved the highest overall accuracy (0.85, Table 3); all models were much weaker on the Not Present and Cannot Tell labels, and several fabricated content — most strikingly Claude-3.5 generating alt text in 32% of Cannot Tell cases and then evaluating its own fabrication (§5.2). A qualitative comparison with five automated checkers (§6) leads to a sensible proposal for a three-tier hybrid workflow. This is a useful, transparently documented benchmark on an important problem. My concerns are with the validation chain underneath the headline numbers: how separable two of the four labels actually are at the input level, how many independent judges stand behind the ground truth, whose reading experience that ground truth represents, and how much of the measured accuracy was tuned on, or is an artefact of, the evaluation protocol itself.
evidence_items.title: PREreview of "Benchmarking PDF Accessibility Evaluation A Dataset and Framework for Assessing Automated and LLM-Based Approaches for Accessibility Testing"

evidence_items.summary: Multi-subject personalized image generation aims to compose multiple distinct reference identities into a coherent scene while preserving their prompt-specified interactions. Existing generators frequently exhibit subject-binding failures as scene complexity scales: omitting requested entities (Existence), blending visual attributes across subjects (Appearance), or misassigning actions and spatial relations (Interaction). Compounding this modeling bottleneck, existing evaluation metrics, which are designed primarily for single-subject similarity or holistic image preference, align only weakly with human judgment on these coupled errors, and several degrade toward random agreement as the number of interacting subjects increases. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce the Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark and Evaluator (MIBE), a unified framework pairing a factorized benchmark (MIB) with a reference-conditioned evaluator (MIE). MIB systematically varies subject count, human-/object-heavy composition, and relation type (non-contact, occlusion, and physical interaction) within a decoupled two-tier data regime: MIB-Silver, a 60K-pair training corpus annotated via a rubric-guided dual-VLM protocol, and MIB-Gold, a 4,020-pair evaluation suite annotated under a double-blind human protocol across six state-of-the-art generators spanning both seen and held-out unseen architectures. Trained exclusively on MIB-Silver with a dual-head objective that jointly predicts pairwise preference rankings and facet-level diagnostics, MIE achieves 0.922 overall pairwise agreement with human consensus on MIB-Gold, including 0.982 on seen generators and 0.884 on held-out unseen generators. Using MIBE for cross-generator diagnosis, we quantify systematic binding bottlenecks across modern generators, providing reproducible benchmark infrastructure and interpretable supervision for future model alignment.
evidence_items.title: MIBE: Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark and Evaluator for Personalized Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: As language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, they must coordinate with others over long horizons in open-ended interactive tasks. Yet existing evaluations rarely test these demands together, focusing instead on single-agent tasks, short interactions, or highly structured multi-agent settings. We introduce $alem$, a JAX-based benchmark for open-ended multi-agent coordination built on Craftax-like dynamics. Alem embeds procedurally generated coordination tasks, soft specialisation, communication, and controllable coordination difficulty into a long-horizon survival world with exploration, crafting, trading, and combat. We evaluate $13$ LLMs zero-shot within homogeneous teams, with trained MARL agents as reference points. Current LLM agents remain far from solving alem, averaging only ~6% normalised return, but their failures are not uniform. On the hardest coordination setting, zero-shot Gemini-3.1-Pro-High approaches MARL agents trained for one billion steps, while GPT-5.4-High achieves strong base-task reward but much lower coordination reward. This contrast shows that individual task competence does not imply coordination competence. Further experiments reveal that communication is the largest contributor to coordination, while memory and reasoning help when used to maintain multi-step plans. In heterogeneous teams, however, combining different models improves base-task progress but lowers coordination reward relative to their homogeneous counterparts. Overall, our results identify coordination as a distinct bottleneck for frontier LLM agents, separate from single-agent capabilities. Alem makes this bottleneck measurable and provides a controlled testbed for developing agents that communicate, allocate roles, and execute shared plans. Code is available at https://github.com/alem-world/alem-env, with LLM traces and a leaderboard at https://alem-world.github.io.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination in Language Agents
