evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Missing data are common in clinical datasets, and imputation performance depends on the dataset and downstream classifier. Feature scaling is usually fixed rather than evaluated experimentally. We investigated whether imputation effects on classification performance depend on scaling and classifier. Methods We used the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic (WBCD) and Pima Indians Diabetes datasets, simulating missingness under a missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism at a target rate of 20%. Mean, median, and MICE-style iterative single imputation were crossed with three scaling strategies (none, standard, robust) and three classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, radial basis function support vector machine [SVM]). Iterative imputation produced one completed dataset per run without pooling using Rubin’s rules. Imputers and scalers were fitted exclusively on training partitions. Five-fold stratified cross-validation repeated five times, with three missingness masks per split, yielded 75 matched split-mask units and 2,025 evaluations per dataset. ROC-AUC was the primary outcome. Analysis used sum-coded ordinary least-squares models with split-cluster-robust covariance and paired comparisons with cluster-bootstrap intervals. Inference was exploratory. Results In WBCD, scaling and classifier choice dominated ROC-AUC variation. Scaling effects were largest for SVM (none versus standard: −0.0219; 95% CI − 0.0267 to − 0.0175), smaller for logistic regression (− 0.0034), and absent for random forest. Marginal imputation differences were at most 0.0009; the largest conditional paired difference was approximately 0.0017. In Pima, SVM performance depended on the imputation-scaling combination: median imputation with robust scaling yielded mean ROC-AUC of 0.757, compared with 0.799 using standard scaling.
evidence_items.title: Does the Effect of Missing-Data Imputation on Classification Performance Depend on Feature Scaling? A Factorial Study Across Classifiers and Clinical Benchmark Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate RNA secondary structure prediction is essential for understanding RNA function, molecular interactions, and regulatory mechanisms across diverse biological processes. Reported performance for RNA secondary structure predic-tors is difficult to compare because studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, splits and metrics. We present a unified benchmark for RNA secondary structure prediction and evaluate 16 representative methods spanning end-to-end deep models, hybrid models with thermodynamic or structural constraints, and pretrained RNA foundation models. Across five settings, intra-dataset, cross-dataset, cross-family, length generalization and pseudoknot prediction, performance rankings vary markedly with evaluation protocol, and no single method dominates all settings. Methods incorporating biophysical priors or explicit structural constraints, together with some pretrained models, are generally more robust under distribution shift, whereas long RNAs and pseudoknots remain challenging for most predictors.
evidence_items.title: A unified benchmark of deep learning methods for RNA secondary structure prediction

evidence_items.summary: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts.
evidence_items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling <em>What</em> Is Fake

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Problems with plant diseases put global food supply at risk; they result in many crops not being able to produce as much or in lower quality than would otherwise be produced. Many small-scale farmers have difficulty accurately and in a timely manner diagnosing disease because of the high expense and limited availability of traditional inspection methods. This study suggests using a novel framework based on agentic artificial intelligence (AI), which incorporates deep learning-based visual analysis and the use of relevant context within the environment, to achieve new levels of intelligent crop health evaluation. The proposed solution is a collaborative multi-agent architecture where dedicated agents can independently complete all steps: automated image preprocessing, automated disease classification, environmental risk assessment, and treatment recommendations. The study employs MobileNetV2 as its backbone because of its lightweight design and low computational requirements, making it possible to use within the resource-limited agriculture environment. To further enhance the quality of diagnostic testing over the long term, there is an added adaptive learning component involved that incorporates feedback from the previous learning cycles. The PlantVillage dataset was used for an empirical analysis and showed in the proposed methodology has a total overall accuracy of 95.32% for the classification. The macro-AVG. for precision 0.95, recall 0.95 and F1 Score 0.95 are indicate the ability to predict well, with stable convergence. The system performs computations with less energy than other systems and can be deployed in a real-time manner on small devices. The transition from intelligent decision support systems to disease diagnostics will be an important milestone toward evolving scalable and precise agricultural systems as well as future sustainable crop production.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Based Plant Disease Detection System

evidence_items.summary: Optical sol-gel environmental pH sensors have been applied for air evaluation in exhibition halls of the Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales (Madrid, Spain). Sensor synthesis and calibration was undertaken following a previous patent by some of the present authors. Monitoring was carried out for one full year to check the influence of meteorological seasons as well as quality of surrounding outdoor air to a big avenue located in downtown Madrid and close to the museum. Particular sites selected for sensor positions were inside showcases, under the free environment of exhibition halls, and outdoor façades of the building, for comparison purposes. pH recordings showed that exhibition halls near the outdoor air entrance had slightly low pH values, which can be attributed to outdoor pollution. However, halls located far from air entrance had neutral conditions. Concerning showcases tested, some of them showed slightly acidic pH while others were moderately acidic due to natural goods exhibited and/or to materials with which showcases were made. pH values recorded allowed the museum to make some decisions on its preventive conservation strategy.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains city-wide maps of the mean annual number of hours with heat stress, expressed by the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), for the urbanized area of Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany (approx. 10 × 7 km) at 1 × 1 m spatial resolution. The maps are derived from hourly street-level UTCI simulations for 2019–2022 (35,064 hourly time steps) presented in Briegel et al. (2024, Geosci. Model Dev., https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-17-1667-2024 ). Model. UTCI was computed from four machine-learning sub-models emulating numerical urban climate models: multi-layer perceptrons emulating a surface energy balance model (SUEWS) for air temperature and relative humidity at the neighbourhood scale (500 × 500 m, 2 m a.g.l.), a U-Net emulating the building-resolved mean radiant temperature model SOLWEIG (1 × 1 m, 1.1 m a.g.l.), and a random forest model for wind speed. The model was forced with observations from an urban rooftop weather station of the University of Freiburg. Evaluated against a dense street-level sensor network in Freiburg, the combined model has a mean absolute error of 2.3 K in UTCI. Content. For each pixel, the files give the mean number of hours per year (averaged over 2019–2022; May-September) in which UTCI fell within a given heat stress class, separately for day and night: – moderate heat stress (26 °C ≤ UTCI < 32 °C) – strong heat stress (32 °C ≤ UTCI < 38 °C) – very strong heat stress (38 °C ≤ UTCI < 46 °C) – extreme heat stress (UTCI ≥ 46 °C) as well as cumulative hours with UTCI ≥ 26 °C and UTCI ≥ 32 °C. Day and night are defined as [e.g. solar elevation angle > 0° / ≤ 0°]. Units: hours per year. Building footprints and pixels outside the model domain are set to NoData ([NA]). Format. GeoTIFF, 1 m resolution. See README.txt for details. Related resources. Model code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7974472 .
evidence_items.title: Street-level UTCI heat stress hours for Freiburg im Breisgau (Germany) at 1 m resolution, 2019–2022: day- and night-time maps by UTCI heat stress class

evidence_items.summary: DEEGMUX is a low-cost, open-source hardware system for high-fidelity, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing of EEG classification algorithms on resource-constrained edge devices. It addresses a common limitation in Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) research, where validating machine learning models typically relies on costly EEG equipment or on simulations that fail to reproduce real-world electronic characteristics. The system comprises two boards: an EEG Demultiplexer Board that converts a multiplexed EEG signal into 8 parallel channels, and an EEG Acquisition and Processing Board built around an ADS1299 24-bit ADC interfaced with an Arduino Nano 33 BLE. This setup enables real EEG datasets — such as the PhysioNet Motor Imagery dataset — to be used to generate precisely timed electronic signals. Characterization demonstrated high signal fidelity, with a Mean Squared Error of 1.7·10⁻¹⁰ V² and a Signal-to-Noise Ratio of 16 dB relative to the original digital data. An EEGNet motor-imagery classifier evaluated on hardware-acquired signals showed a negligible accuracy difference of (−0.3 ± 5)% with respect to evaluation on the original data, confirming that the emulation chain preserves classification-relevant features. DEEGMUX provides a scalable, reproducible, and affordable platform for rigorously testing edge-deployed CNN models against realistic electronic inputs, accelerating the transition from simulation to robust real-world BCI deployment.
evidence_items.title: Reproducible testing for embedded BCIs: a demultiplexing PCB and acquisition system for EEG signal emulation

evidence_items.summary: The NanoSSD database comprises curated ecotoxicity records for engineered nanomaterials (ENMs) across four environmental compartments: freshwater, marine water, soil and sediment. The database was developed to support Species Sensitivity Distribution (SSD) analysis, the derivation of hazardous concentrations (HCs) and predicted no-effect concentrations (PNECs), and the environmental risk assessment of ENMs. Ecotoxicity records were compiled from previously published scientific studies, established ecotoxicological databases and curated datasets, including NanoE-Tox and the US EPA ECOTOX Knowledgebase. Additional literature searches were conducted to extend the coverage of terrestrial and sediment-dwelling organisms. The database includes metal, metal oxide, carbon-based and graphene-based nanomaterials, as well as quantum dots. Where available, information is provided on nanomaterial composition, primary particle size, size category, morphology, surface coating and functionalisation, taxonomic classification, species, exposure duration, experimental conditions, toxicity endpoints and bibliographic references. Additional physicochemical properties of the exposure medium, including soil pH, organic carbon content, water holding capacity and cation exchange capacity, are provided for terrestrial ecotoxicity records where available. The toxicity indicators include effect concentrations (EC10, EC20 and EC50), lethal concentrations (LC10, LC20 and LC50), no-observed-effect concentrations (NOECs) and lowest-observed-effect concentrations (LOECs). Toxicity concentrations are expressed in mg/L for aquatic compartments, mg/kg for soil and mg/kg dry weight for sediment. The dataset serves as the underlying ecotoxicity database of NanoSSD, a web application developed for the construction, statistical evaluation and visualisation of SSDs for engineered nanomaterials.
evidence_items.title: NanoSSD: A Curated Ecotoxicity Database for Species Sensitivity Distribution Analysis of Engineered Nanomaterials

evidence_items.summary: Abstract   Background: Food systems account for roughly a third of global greenhouse-gas emissions, and demand-side change must complement supply-side mitigation. Carbon footprint labels are a scalable lever, yet ecologically valid evidence from live commercial retail environments remains scarce. This article reports the design and results of a consumer pilot that embedded product-level carbon footprint labelling and digital nudging in the German online store of one of the leading European drugstore retailers, with randomised controlled trials built in. Methods: An end-to-end, transferable methodology combined stakeholder mapping, three participatory co-design laboratories, lifecycle assessment-based labelling, a six-step campaign design framework, a discrete-choice experiment and a Bayesian sequential A/B testing platform. Five campaigns were delivered between August 2025 and September 2026 across the retailer’s website, app, newsletter, a mobile messaging channel and paid native advertising, and evaluated through engagement analytics, eight randomised comparisons, the choice experiment and product-level sales. Results: Carbon footprint information reliably attracted attention. The first campaign exceeded its reach target, and its website  placement outperformed the retailer’s informational campaign benchmark. In the newsletter test, the emotional subject line outperformed the informational one, with a 100% probability of being best in both customer segments. A gamified quiz engaged a younger audience well above the channel benchmark, and three data-storytelling framings of the same carbon difference drew similar attention but differed in onward click-through. Purchasing did not change in the first campaigns, but two of the three products promoted in the final campaign outperformed their category year on year, an indicative purchasing response.
evidence_items.title: Design and first results of a German online retail pilot of carbon footprint eco-labelling and digital nudging to promote sustainable food consumption

evidence_items.summary: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.
evidence_items.title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination

evidence_items.summary: Background: Deep learning fundus classifiers often perform well internally, but duplicated images, inconsistent labels, acquisition differences and poor threshold transfer can undermine their reliability. We assess nine-class classifiers beyond internal accuracy, using a data audit, frozen-model external evaluation and an anatomy-guided specialist. Methods: Nine-class experts (ConvNeXt-Small, EfficientNetV2-Small, DenseNet169) were trained with three seeds. Auditing 5,318 images for exact duplicates and cross-label conflicts removed 464 conflict groups (942 images) and six same-label copies, leaving 4,370 images. An anatomy-guided glaucoma specialist read disc-centred crops with vessel and disc/cup segmentation maps, plus cup-to-disc features. Frozen models were evaluated on RFMiD and JSIEC, and a prespecified comparison on REFUGE was replicated on ORIGA, G1020 and PAPILA. Results: ConvNeXt-Small reached an internal accuracy of 0.910, macro-F1 of 0.917 and AUC of 0.982; disc and cup Dice scores were 0.966 and 0.915. Across seeds, the fixed anatomy-guided mix left internal accuracy unchanged relative to equal soft voting (-0.001) but raised mean external closed-set accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on RFMiD (positive in two of three seeds) and 2.3 on JSIEC. On REFUGE (800 photographs) it improved balanced accuracy by 7.4 percentage points (95% CI 5.1 to 9.5), and by 2.1 on ORIGA, with positive gains on G1020 and PAPILA. Thresholds transferred poorly (REFUGE sensitivity 0.950, specificity 0.411). Conclusions: Retinal classifiers should be judged by data-quality auditing, anatomy-informed modelling and multi-cohort evaluation. Anatomy-guided fusion improved transfer at no internal cost, but gains varied by cohort and thresholds did not transfer, so internal metrics alone do not establish reliable performance.
evidence_items.title: Data-Quality-Aware Fundus Classification with Anatomy-Guided Glaucoma Assessment and Cross-Dataset Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Existing research on Aha moments in large language models has largely focused on reflective expressions or final revision outcomes, leaving their role in the visible reasoning process insufficiently characterized. Rebus puzzles encode answers through character forms, spatial arrangements, and homophony. Reinterpreting key details may trigger Aha moments and shifts in the reasoning process and candidate answers. We introduce AhaPro, a process-level benchmark that uses rebus puzzles to examine how models reorganize evidence and revise answers through Aha moments. The framework represents CoT as sequences of candidate answers, evidence, and verification states, using hierarchical metrics to assess conflict detection, state improvement, and subsequent adoption. Across eleven models, we observe frequent failures to adopt better states discovered during Aha moments, alongside adopted revisions that leave state quality unchanged or reduce it. Models also detect conflicts without subsequently achieving an effective revision. Further paired interventions suggest that prior reasoning context may hinder effective revision after conflict detection, while multi-branch search highlights answer selection as a bottleneck between correct-answer discovery and successful correction.
evidence_items.title: AhaPro: A Process-level Rebus benchmark for probing Aha moments in LLM reasoning

evidence_items.summary: As frontier AI models and agents are deployed more broadly in the real world, marketing is emerging as one of their largest applications. Marketing teams use AI models to produce brand assets like website copy and social media posts, while consumers' agents autonomously discover products, research purchases, and navigate websites. However, evaluating marketing capability is difficult because unlike areas like software development, customer support, or legal review where ground truth is more objectively defined, marketing is subjective, and output quality is judged based on taste and brand. We introduce Marketing-Bench, the first open-source marketing benchmark, which pairs discriminative tasks (detecting brand anomalies) with generative tasks (remediation), while keeping answers verifiable. Marketing-Bench tests five key pillars: factuality, consistency, coherence, structure, and brand voice, all crucial elements for good brand content on the web. We find that frontier models are far from solving the benchmark: the average model corrects only about half of the introduced issues (53.1%), whereas a marketing expert corrects nearly all of them. Even the strongest, GPT-6 Astra, reaches only 74.8%, with Claude Opus and Fable, Gemini Argon, and GPT-6 Sol falling well short. These findings suggest that marketing capabilities are less mature than adoption implies, and that principled evaluation should precede further scaling of usage. Marketing-Bench is a first step toward "frontier marketing models" with superhuman marketing performance.
evidence_items.title: Marketing-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Models and Agents on Real-World Marketing Capabilities

evidence_items.summary: The FBT spectral-capacity action is the heat trace of one specified geometric Dirac operator at fixed spectral resolution. This paper states its domain and trace hypotheses, exact first and second variations, stationarity tests, coupled relative-torus 4 + 2 expression, and complete finite-computation requirements. The current application uses the embeddingto-operator map already supplied by DCQ6 and FBT10D on the closed coherent product. No second source map is required. The degree-24 regular magnetic realization, its singular-end analysis and the separate torus numerical benchmark are removed from the main development. Their removal leaves the functional and the relative-torus geometry intact. The global line-extension obstruction is retained to explain this separation. The inherited twist, its closed domain and all metric, spin and connection variations are used together. Exact fibre integration preserves the full heat trace; the four-dimensional quadratic action and normal stability certificates are cited from FBT10D with their original scope. General spectral error bounds retain feedback through omitted modes and distinguish affine connection tests from nonlinear geometric families. A final ledger separates established results from resolution selection, balance-layer selection, full nonlinear control and real-time interpretation. This revision introduces no new numerical sign certificate or physical mass prediction.
evidence_items.title: FBT10A: The Spectral–Capacity Action of the Fracture–Berry–Tension Framework

evidence_items.summary: This dataset supports the study entitled “Design and User-Centered Evaluation of a Dual-Mode Virtual Reality System for Scenario-Based Hotel English Learning.” The study involved 152 undergraduate students majoring in hospitality management, with 76 participants assigned to immersive virtual reality (IVR) and 76 to desktop virtual reality (DVR). Both configurations provided equivalent instructional content and scenario-based learning activities while differing in their display and input methods. The dataset contains de-identified questionnaire responses collected after participants completed the assigned learning activities. The evaluation employed three instruments: the System Usability Scale (SUS), the User Experience Questionnaire–Short Version (UEQ-S), and a Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)-based questionnaire assessing perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. The data were used to examine differences between IVR and DVR in perceived system usability, pragmatic and hedonic user experience quality, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The increasing global deployment of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems needs robust, scalable, and automated inspection technologies capable of detecting a wide range of panel flaws under a variety of operating situations. The lack of comprehensive, multi-modal, publicly available annotated datasets is a major obstacle preventing advancement in this field. We introduce SolarFCD, a harmonized multi-modal dataset of solar panel defects created by methodically combining and reconciling three publicly accessible datasets covering two imaging modalities. Following near-duplicate removal, the dataset comprises 3,742 unique real images, expanded to 6,651 through targeted augmentation of the three under-represented classes; augmentation was applied to the training and validation partitions, and all test images are unique real observations. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test splits at an 80:10:10 ratio through methodical label mapping, near-duplicate removal, and targeted augmentation of minority classes. Sixteen classification architectures from five design families were trained and assessed on the dataset to provide repeatable benchmark baselines. With an accuracy of 86.93%, precision of 88.79%, recall of 88.72%, and F1-score of 88.27%, ResNet101V2 performed the best overall. Per-class results showed balanced detection across all four defect categories within a narrow performance band. To promote open and repeatable research in automated PV inspection and solar energy operations and maintenance, the dataset, annotation files, and baseline code are made openly available.
evidence_items.title: SolarFCD: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Solar Fault Classification in Photovoltaic Systems

evidence_items.summary: Static public benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically have fixed and narrow test distributions. Their repeated reuse encourages benchmark-specific tuning, making reported performance reflect adaptation to the fixed test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. In addition, a single aggregate score cannot fully characterize model capabilities across distinct temporal structures and input relationships. We propose CaFE (Capability-Focused Evaluation), a refreshable evaluation extension grounded in original benchmark data that enriches static benchmarks with structural diversity and enriches single-score black-box evaluation with multi-dimensional, capability-oriented assessment. CaFE first profiles the original benchmark and defines eight Structural Features (SFs) that characterize its temporal structure. For each SF, it resamples the original data according to its structural support, removes edge-of-distribution samples, and augments the retained samples by varying the SF's salience, producing samples with different structural profiles. After filtering out out-of-distribution samples while preserving diversity, CaFE yields a refreshed evaluation set. TSFMs are then evaluated on this set using both conventional forecast-error metrics and our proposed intervention-response metrics, giving each model a per-feature capability profile alongside endpoint accuracy. Experiments on GIFT-Eval and FEV-Mini20 show that CaFE yields stable evaluation results and reveals per-feature strengths and weaknesses that a single aggregate score hides. Moreover, on genuine data filtered by structural condition, models selected by CaFE outperform those chosen by the aggregate leaderboard. CaFE therefore makes model selection conditional on the structural response of interest.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Capability-Focused Evaluation with Structural Diversity for Time Series Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Nighttime aerial image enhancement is constrained by the scarcity of aligned normal-light targets. Acquiring such targets from moving UAVs is difficult, and simple darkening of daytime images underrepresents the sensor noise, localized lighting, and uneven exposure of real nighttime captures. Generating normal-light references from real nighttime observations offers a practical way to fill this supervision gap. AeroNight pairs 1,200 real nighttime aerial RGB images with generated references selected through manual screening, preserving real imaging degradation in the inputs. This setting motivates AeroLLE, a lightweight two-stage framework whose context-aware Base Enhancer combines local processing with scene-level frequency information to recover visibility. Spatially Adaptive Exposure-Color Calibration (SAECC) then refines the base prediction through bounded low-resolution RGB gain and bias fields. AeroLLE achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated methods on both held-out test sets, reaching 17.62/17.89 dB PSNR and 0.5190/0.4964 SSIM on Test 1/Test 2, respectively. The model uses 255.24K parameters and 2.47G FLOPs, reducing FLOPs by 85.4\% relative to Multinex and improving PSNR by 1.56 dB on Test 2. AeroNight provides the first benchmark for pseudo-supervised nighttime aerial enhancement, and AeroLLE shows that generated references can support compact enhancement models.
evidence_items.title: AeroLLE: Nighttime Aerial Image Enhancement with Generated Supervision

evidence_items.summary: This protocol describes a scoping review to identify and synthesize outcomes and measurement instruments used in research on manuscript peer review, forming the first phase of the Primary Evaluation outcomEs for Research on peer review – A Core Outcome Set (PEER-COS) initiative. Guided by the JBI methodology for scoping reviews, the review will include English-language systematic reviews and empirical studies published from 1986 onward across biomedical sciences, health sciences, social sciences, economics, and healthcare-related industries. Comprehensive bibliographic database searches will be supplemented by searches of preprint servers and grey literature sources. Study selection and data extraction will incorporate artificial intelligence tools, including otto-SR and ChatGPT, with predefined quality checks and human verification. Extracted data will describe study characteristics, peer review outcomes and their definitions or operationalizations, and measurement instruments and their reported measurement properties. Findings will be summarized descriptively, and conceptually similar outcomes will be consolidated and organized into broader domains to generate candidate items for a subsequent Delphi consensus study. The review will provide the evidence base for developing a core outcome set intended to improve consistency in outcome selection and reporting, facilitate comparisons across studies, and strengthen evidence synthesis in manuscript peer review research.
evidence_items.title: Primary Evaluation outcomEs for Research on peer review – A Core Outcome Set (PEER-COS): A Scoping Review to Inform Item Development  (Protocol)

evidence_items.summary: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is an emerging technology in orthodontics that facilitates the identification and assessment of dental abnormalities through automated image analysis. Its application may support early recognition of malocclusion and preventive orthodontic care. Objectives: To evaluate the role of artificial intelligence in the early identification of orthodontic abnormalities and assess its diagnostic performance compared with clinical orthodontic examination. Study Design & Setting: Descriptive cross-sectional study conducted at the Department of Orthodontics, Shahida Islam Dental College, Lodhran from March 2026 to September 2026. Methodology: A total of 150 patients aged 6–18 years were included using a non-probability consecutive sampling technique. Demographic information and orthodontic findings were recorded through clinical examination and standardized intraoral photographs. Dental photographs were analysed using an AI-based assessment system, and its findings were compared with clinical diagnoses established by an experienced orthodontist. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, diagnostic accuracy, and Cohen's kappa coefficient were calculated. Results: The mean age of participants was 11.8 ± 3.4 years, with males comprising 52.0% of the sample. Dental crowding was the most frequent orthodontic abnormality (42.0%), followed by increased overjet (26.0%). Artificial intelligence identified abnormalities in 77.3% of participants. The diagnostic assessment demonstrated a sensitivity of 89.0%, specificity of 65.6%, positive predictive value of 90.5%, negative predictive value of 61.8%, and overall accuracy of 84.0%. Agreement between AI assessment and clinical examination was 84.0%, with a reported Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.59. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence demonstrated promising performance in identifying orthodontic abnormalities and may support early orthodontic screening.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Orthodontic Prevention

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for acute cervical spine fracture (CSFx) detection, but its performance across diverse computed tomography (CT) protocols in unselected emergency workflows requires validation. This study evaluated an AI application on dedicated non-contrast cervical spine CTs and conducted a ‘stress test’ on contrast-enhanced whole-body trauma CTs. Methods: This retrospective study included 724 consecutive adults undergoing cervical spine or whole-body CT at a Level I trauma center (November 2023–February 2025). Disagreements with retrospective review defaulted to the original senior-validated clinical report, reflecting agreement with routine practice rather than an independent expert consensus. Results: Overall, 79/724 patients had acute CSFx (10.9% prevalence), including 54/627 (8.6%) imaged for acute initial trauma. On non-contrast CTs (n = 298), the AI achieved 88.0% sensitivity (95% CI: 76.2–94.4), 88.3% specificity, 60.3% positive predictive value (PPV), and 97.3% negative predictive value (NPV); in the acute-initial-trauma non-contrast subgroup (n = 204), sensitivity was 80.0% (20/25; 95% CI: 60.9–91.1). On contrast-enhanced CTs (n = 426), sensitivity was 86.2%, whereas specificity was lower (75.1%), associated with arterial opacification artifacts and protocol-group differences. Exact vertebral level localization was achieved in 60/69 (87.0%) detected positive examinations and 60/79 (75.9%) fracture-positive examinations. Conclusions: Evaluated for agreement with routine senior-validated clinical reports, the AI showed high sensitivity and NPV in an unselected cohort, suggesting potential triage utility, though acute-initial-trauma non-contrast sensitivity was lower (80.0%) and workflow impact remains unmeasured. Arterial-phase acquisitions were associated with higher false-positive rates, warranting protocol-aware interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Real-World Clinical Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence Application for Acute Cervical Spine Fracture Detection on CT

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Poland has 17 designated adult trauma centres but no national trauma registry. This study assessed which trauma data elements required by the American College of Surgeons (ACS) are available in Polish public data sources and what these sources reveal about the care of injured patients. Methods In this cross-sectional gap analysis, 17 verifiable requirements from the ACS Trauma Systems Consultation Guide, the 2022 Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient, the National Trauma Data Standard, the Trauma Quality Improvement Program and the Utstein template were mapped against Polish sources and graded on a five-level scale. Sources were National Health Fund portals and open hospital data (2017–2025), Police, Statistics Poland and air rescue reports. In-hospital mortality in injury-related diagnosis-related groups was analysed; trauma centres were compared using indirect standardisation and funnel plots. Five established trauma registries served as comparators. Results Of 17 requirements, one was fully available in public data; the gap was small for one, moderate for one, large for four and critical for nine; one was not applicable. No source contained Abbreviated Injury Scale codes, physiological parameters, process times or linked 30-day outcomes. In injury-related groups the share of patients aged ≥ 65 years rose from 31.3% (2017) to 47.8% (2025); they accounted for 75.7% of in-hospital deaths in 2025. Multiple-injury groups (1002–1466 stays per year) were billed by trauma centres in 99.1–99.8% of cases. Standardised mortality ratios of centres ranged from 0.49 to 2.10; six of 17 lay outside 95% control limits. In operative severe head injury, the observed-to-expected mortality ratio was 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.92) in trauma centres and 1.05 (1.03–1.07) in other hospitals, but trauma centres transferred more patients onward (17.8% vs 11.9%).
evidence_items.title: No registry, no benchmark: a nationwide cross-sectional gap analysis of trauma care data in Poland against American College of Surgeons standards

evidence_items.summary: Smart parking systems guide drivers to free spaces through mobile interfaces whose usefulness depends on the accuracy and lead time of the underlying occupancy forecasts. We benchmark seven models—random forest (RF), XGBoost, LightGBM, a feed-forward neural network (NN), an LSTM, a temporal convolutional network (TCN), and a transformer—on a full year of real data: 112,830 observations from five LoRaWAN-instrumented spaces at the University of Prishtina, Kosovo (June 2024–June 2025). Departing from single-horizon nowcasting, we predict at 15-minute, 1-hour, and 2-hour lead times for both binary occupancy classification and continuous occupancy-ratio regression, under a leakage-free chronological split, with deep models trained to convergence and every result averaged over ten seeds with significance testing. The value of machine learning proves strongly horizon-dependent: because occupancy is highly autocorrelated, a zero-cost persistence baseline matches the best learned model up to one hour ahead, and only at two hours do six of the seven models beat it significantly (best long shortterm memory (LSTM) 79.82% vs. 76.32%, p < 10-10). For regression the sequence models lead at every horizon (R2 = 0.686 at one hour) and the gradient-boosted trees outrank RF. An ablation shows historical (autocorrelation) features supply almost all of the signal, corroborated by SHAP and permutation importance. A resource analysis is counterintuitive: RF trains fastest yet yields the largest model (165 MB), while the compact sequence models (~0.2 MB) are far more deployable. These results give realistic, persistence-aware guidance for smart-parking services.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning for LoRaWAN Smart Parking: A Multi-Horizon Occupancy Prediction Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Fixed Benford conformity bands classify every unit as nonconforming when each observation rests on a few figures, and ratios built from the tested amounts can be associated with a digit statistic through arithmetic alone. We propose a panel-based benchmark that builds a bank-year index of first-digit deviation from five reported amounts and judges conformity and regression coefficients against a rotation reference, which preserves each bank’s ratios and growth path and randomises its scale. In simulations without departures, the benchmark flagged 3.7% to 3.9% of units at the bank level and 5.6% to 7.2% pooled, but its power against altered leading digits was at most 0.07 for a single bank and 0.26 pooled. We illustrate it on twelve Indonesian banks with four fraud hexagon proxies. The pooled deviation lay at the 67th percentile of the benchmark, and one of 13 units exceeded its 95th percentile. In fixed-effects models the benchmark reproduced about 17% of the leverage coefficient, and the remainder could not be distinguished from zero; the other proxies were indistinguishable from zero, with minimum detectable effects 1.7 to 3.6 times the estimates, so the illustration shows the limits of such a panel. The extracted amounts do not satisfy the balance identity within 1% of assets in 33 of 72 bank-years, and the proxies are unvalidated, so results are exploratory. Restricting the panel to the 39 bank-years that reconcile within 0.1% left these conclusions unchanged. Digit-based studies using ratios built from tested figures should benchmark associations against arithmetic dependence.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Benford’s Law: A Rotation Benchmark for First-Digit Screening in Small Bank Panels

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous AI agents that read email, browse the web, call tools, and delegate to other agents turn a model's text-following behaviour into real-world actions. This makes prompt injection, where attacker-controlled content is mistaken for instructions, a direct route to data exfiltration, record tampering, and privilege escalation. Defences that try to make the model itself resistant are probabilistic and have been shown to fail against adaptive attackers. This paper takes the complementary position that an agent should be secured by the enforcement layer around the model, on the assumption that the model can be manipulated. It proposes a threat model and an attack taxonomy for agentic workflows, defines six defence designs from prompt-level filtering to a layered architecture of scoped capabilities, plan-locking, information-flow labels, and targeted human confirmation, and evaluates them in a simulated agent environment with eight tasks, fifteen tools at four privilege levels, and eight attack classes. The model is represented as a stochastic policy that follows an injected instruction with a given probability, and the defences are deterministic policy code. Without defences, attacks succeeded in about 60% of episodes at a follow probability of 0.6 and 77% for persistent memory poisoning. Prompt-level defences reduced this to 3% to 4% for tool-output injection but not for memory poisoning, and their effectiveness fell as detector recall fell (3.6% to 23.9% mean success from recall 0.85 to 0). Tool allowlists blocked out-of-scope tools but left in-scope abuse at 60%. Plan-locking with information-flow labels reduced every attack to zero except in-scope record tampering (30%), whereas scoped capabilities alone left exfiltration to a compromised known contact at 60%.
evidence_items.title: Securing Autonomous Agentic AI Workflows Against Prompt Injection and Privilege Escalation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Archaeology has many competing theories but, at the meso-scale where most interpretation occurs, few sound tests. We advance an agentic agent-based modelling (agentic-ABM) framework in which an AI research agent works with an archaeologist throughout testing. The AI agents stay outside the model, whose simulated agents follow fixed rules. The research agent synthesises literature, formalises published positions as rules, labels every parameter as cited or assumed, executes scenarios, runs sensitivity analyses, and docks the model: two independent AI agents on different large language models re-implement it blind. The archaeologist directs research, approves rules, tests code and evaluates outcomes. The case is a long-standing debate: the labour and cooperation behind Bronze Age Sardinia's 7,167 nuraghi (Nurnet data); 26 of 29 scenarios draw on published work, 13 directly. We develop a protocol for testing theory with agentic-ABM, extending docking to AI agents. Both re-implementations reproduce the labour results in sampled runs of both engines; construction-time differences trace mostly to specification ambiguities, and the second arm falls just short of the time criterion. Docking verifies implementation, not historical validity; results are bounds under stated assumptions. Agentic-ABM turns speculative theory into auditable, replicable, comparative tests of which pasts are more likely, not which happened.
evidence_items.title: Testing Archaeological Theory Using Agentic-ABM: A Case from Nuragic Sardinia

organizations: School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Institute of Communication and Computer Systems (ICCS), National Technical University of Athens
evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence is evolving from the passive content generation of Generative AI (GenAI) to Agentic AI (AgAI) systems which are increasingly characterized by autonomy, adaptability, and goal-driven reasoning. Unlike traditional GenAI, AgAI systems are capable of perception, planning, and independent action. This shift introduces a unique class of sociotechnical risks, including goal misalignment, cascading operational errors, and security vulnerabilities. This paper reviews the AgAI landscape, examines its architectural components (planning, memory, action, and multi-agent collaboration) and its transformative potential across key sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, robotics, and software development. By analyzing existing corporate and regulatory governance frameworks, the paper identifies gaps in accountability, liability, and real-time intervention. We argue that establishing trustworthy AgAI requires a shift from regulating content to constraining autonomous consequences, and propose seven research and governance challenges focusing on dynamic alignment, responsibility attribution, verifiable specifications, and standardized benchmarks, to ensure AgAI systems remain aligned with human values.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy agentic AI systems: navigating the risks and governance of autonomous AI

evidence_items.summary: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.
evidence_items.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Solar filaments are cool, dense chromospheric plasma structures held by magnetic field lines above polarity inversion lines. Their destabilization triggers coronal mass ejections and severe space weather hazards. Segmenting individual filaments from ground-based GONG H-alpha observations (2048 x 2048 pixels) is challenging due to low contrast, turbulent fibrils, delicate barb structures, and annotator boundary variance. In this technical report, we describe SolarFilNet-V4, a targeted segmentation framework developed for the MAGFiLO 1.0 benchmark (Solar Filament Segmentation Challenge 2026). Our method couples a lightweight Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT-v2-B1) backbone with anisotropic curvilinear strip convolutions (k=15) and dual-frequency feed-forward blocks (DFFN) to follow extended flux ropes while capturing thin central spines. A shallow full-resolution convolutional branch operating at 1024 x 1024 preserves high-frequency edge details and mitigates transformer downsampling. We train the network using multi-task supervision over masks, centerline spines, barb boundaries, and pixel-contrastive representations. At test time, we apply 8-fold dihedral test-time augmentation (D4), bilinearly upscale predictions to the native 2048 x 2048 grid, and apply an activity-adaptive post-processing routine that calibrates morphological joining parameters for quiet versus active solar disks. On the official benchmark, SolarFilNet-V4 achieves an out-of-fold validation Panoptic Quality of 0.4340 and a Public Leaderboard score of 0.380. The model contains 15.46M parameters and requires 224.34 GFLOPs per forward pass, reducing parameter count by 36.8% compared to standard ResNet-34 U-Net baselines.
evidence_items.title: SolarFilNet-V4: Multi-Scale Transformer Vision with Physics-Informed Adaptive Post-Processing for Solar Filament Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.
evidence_items.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
