evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide a strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agent-conditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as a scalable counterpart to self-evolving agents, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured.
evidence_items.title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/
evidence_items.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading

evidence_items.summary: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.
evidence_items.title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.
evidence_items.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

evidence_items.summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
evidence_items.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Despite the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in data-intensive disciplines, archaeology lacks public, large-scale benchmarks, and its spatio-temporally fragmented knowledge resists integration into model parameters. Here we introduce ArchaeoBench, a hierarchically structured benchmark built from 63 official excavation reports across 20 Chinese provinces, comprising over 9.2 million training question-answer pairs and 1,698 evaluation questions spanning multiple cognitive levels. Fine-tuning seven open-source LLMs on this benchmark yields substantial gains, approaching commercial baselines on several question types, whereas chain-of-thought prompting brings only marginal improvements on fact- and text-grounded questions, suggesting that archaeological question answering is constrained primarily by access to reliable domain knowledge rather than reasoning depth. Motivated by this finding, we propose a knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation framework that injects curated structured evidence to enhance spatio-temporal and cultural-linkage reasoning. ArchaeoBench converts excavation reports into reusable, machine-readable knowledge infrastructure for the discipline.
evidence_items.title: ArchaeoBench: a large-scale archaeological question-answering benchmark for large language models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) attain high accuracy on medical examinations, yet evaluations rely predominantly on single-best-answer multiple-choice questions and report only overall accuracy. Multiple-response items, termed X-type in China, require selecting every correct option and remain understudied. Whether models err by omitting correct options or by commissioning incorrect ones has yet to be assessed within an opportunity-standardized framework. Objective This study aimed to quantify the accuracy penalty of multiple-response (X-type) items relative to single-select items and to determine, after standardizing for the unequal numbers of correct and incorrect options, whether LLMs lean toward omission or commission. Methods We analyzed 1644 text-based items from 10 examination cohorts (2017‐2026) of the Chinese National Postgraduate Entrance Examination in Clinical Medicine, comprising 1344 single-select items of types A1, A2, A3, and B, and 300 X-type items. Five LLMs, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Doubao Seed-2.1-pro, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini-3.6 Flash, were tested zero-shot bilingually, yielding 16,440 planned responses. Item-type effects were estimated using generalized estimating equations with cluster-robust standard errors, adjusting for model, language, discipline, and cohort. Opportunity-standardized error direction was analyzed 2 ways: an option-level model treating each option as 1 judgment record and the omission-bias index. Results Of 16,440 planned responses, 16,426 (99.91%) were evaluable. X-type accuracy (2527/3000, 84.23%) was markedly below single-select accuracy (12,990/13,426, 96.75%; adjusted odds ratio at GPT-5.6 Sol in Chinese 0.17, 95% CI 0.11‐0.26; P <.001), a gap of 12.52 percentage points observed and 13.55 adjusted, with no statistically significant item type × model or item type × language interaction ( P =.19 and P =.82).
evidence_items.title: Error Direction of Large Language Models on Medical Multiple-Response Questions: Opportunity-Standardized Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Domain ontology construction from unstructured text is a core knowledge-engineering task, and large language models (LLMs) offer a practical route to automating concept and relation extraction. Evidence on how reliably LLMs extract hierarchical and semantic relations under different prompting strategies remains limited for resource-poor, rapidly evolving domains. This study presents a gold-standard benchmark for LLM-based concept and relation extraction and a scripted pipeline that assembles a logically consistent Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontology. Using 19 Chinese university artificial intelligence (AI) course syllabi as a case study, we built a benchmark of 131 concepts and 75 relations of four types through two-author double-blind screening with adjudication (Cohen's κ = 0.707) and an independent blinded audit by two external reviewers (item-level agreement 42/50 and 43/50). Three Chinese LLMs were evaluated under one-shot and decomposed prompting across 114 configurations. On 14 held-out documents, macro concept F1 was 0.42–0.48 (0.51–0.60 on the development set), with a stable Core > Common > Peripheral gradient. Relation extraction was markedly weaker, constrained by concept-granularity mismatch and, among matched predictions, dominated by is-a/prerequisite type confusion. The assembled ontology passes HermiT satisfiability checking and supports downstream knowledge-graph diagnosis. The benchmark, prompts, ontology, and scripts are publicly released.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Concept and Relation Extraction in Ontology Construction: A Benchmark on Chinese Domain-Specific Text

organizations: University of Cincinnati College of Medicine
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Diagnostic benchmarks can reward recognition of a disease family without requiring the specificity of the final diagnosis. We evaluated the separation between broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness in a retrieval augmented language model. Methods This retrospective benchmark evaluated MediDx AI, which couples Claude Sonnet 4.6 with retrieval from seven biomedical sources without fine-tuning, on presentation-only text from 100 consecutive published Massachusetts General Hospital Case Records, issued from 26 October 2023 to 11 June 2026. Published expert discussions, final diagnoses, source tables and images were withheld. Five ranked suggestions were adjudicated under broad concordance and strict correct, partial or incorrect scoring. Case-level proportions and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated. A separate evaluation used 1,273 medical multiple-choice questions, counting unanswered questions as incorrect. Results Broad top-ranked concordance was 71% (95% confidence interval 61.5–79.0%), whereas 53% (43.3–62.5%) of top-ranked diagnoses were strictly correct; 19% were partial and 28% incorrect. Within five suggestions, broad concordance was 88% and strict correctness was 63%. The 18 broadly concordant but partial top-ranked diagnoses accounted for the difference between the two top-ranked outcomes. Failures included missed causative organisms, rare neoplasms and structural conditions; partial responses often omitted an underlying mechanism or a component of a multicomponent diagnosis. Medical question-answering accuracy was 86.5% across all submitted questions, compared with 92.0% among parseable responses; response coverage was 94.0%. Conclusions Broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness describe different aspects of performance. Reporting both, alongside ranked inclusion and response completion, exposes information concealed by aggregate accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic specificity of a retrieval augmented language model on complex clinical cases: a retrospective benchmark study

evidence_items.summary: Background: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to assess risk of bias in randomized trials, but how task-specific fine-tuned models compare with frontier models remains uncertain. Objective: To develop RoB-BERT, a fine-tuned RoB 2 assessment system, and to compare its agreement with human assessments against that of three frontier LLMs. Methods: RoB 2 rates five bias domains and the trial overall as low risk, some concerns or high risk, based on answers to 22 signalling questions. RoB-BERT answers each question, quotes the supporting sentences from the trial report, and applies the official RoB 2 algorithm. We trained RoB-BERT on 5,304 reviewer-checked assessments, none from a test trial, and compared it with Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, each given identical prompts and text, against 419 published human assessments (ROBoto2, LogiMed-RoB and Cochrane reviews) made without AI assistance. Each reference was the single published judgement for that trial, made by one assessor or agreed by two, rather than an expert reference standard, so we also report agreement between two human assessors of the same trial. Results: In ROBoto2, pairs of human assessors who rated the same trial agreed on 61.2% to 64.7% of domain judgements (κ 0.15 to 0.35) and 46.2% to 50.0% of overall judgements (κ 0.15 to 0.17); across the 185 ROBoto2 trials, RoB-BERT agreed with the human judgement on 67.4% (κ 0.35) and 53.5% (κ 0.20). Across all 419 assessments, domain agreement was 67.9% (κ 0.29) for RoB-BERT, 65.0% (κ 0.24) for Claude Fable 5.1, 52.7% (κ 0.21) for GPT-6 Astra and 66.7% (κ 0.26) for Gemini 4 Argon; overall agreement was 46.1% (κ 0.16), 47.3% (κ 0.17), 31.0% (κ 0.03) and 46.5% (κ 0.14), respectively. For domains the reference rated high risk, sensitivity was 22.2% for RoB-BERT, 23.1% for Claude Fable 5.1, 41.9% for GPT-6 Astra and 24.8% for Gemini 4 Argon, with specificity of 92.5%, 92.8%, 80.0% and 95.0%.
evidence_items.title: Task-specific fine-tuning versus frontier large language models for RoB 2 risk of bias assessment: development and external benchmark evaluation of RoB-BERT

evidence_items.summary: Style words such as delve, intricate and meticulous became several times more frequent in English research abstracts after large language models became public. Publicly named as evidence of machine-assisted writing, they have since turned down as a set. The prevailing explanation, deliberate avoidance, predicts that the words named most widely receded furthest, a prediction tested here on every eligible PubMed abstract entered from January 2018 to June 2026 (N = 10,767,846). Thirty such words were compared by segmented regression against two control sets from the same corpus: comparably frequent words that never rose, and emphatic markers from a published metadiscourse inventory. Lexical density, nominalisation, passive voice and hedging were also measured. How widely each word had been named was scored beforehand across fourteen independent inventories. Twenty-nine of the thirty turned down and neither control set did, ruling out corpus drift and a general cooling of evaluative prose. Public naming did not predict the decline to the extent the awareness account requires: a word&rsquo;s earlier rise predicted its fall, naming added nothing with that rise held constant, and the steepest decliners include words on no inventory. The structural features did not turn back. The test is powered to detect an association of the size that account requires, not a weak one, which cannot be excluded. Model turnover or heavier editing of output fits the pattern better than selective avoidance; these data cannot separate them. The visible lexical signal of machine-assisted writing is weakening; the impersonal texture of the prose is not.
evidence_items.title: Delving into Decline: The Rise and Fall of Large Language Model Vocabulary in Biomedical Abstracts, 2018–2026

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most transformative technologies in modern medicine. Its influence is especially visible in clinical areas that generate high-volume digital data, including imaging, electrocardiography, pathology, patient monitoring, and electronic health records. As these data sources continue to expand, AI is increasingly moving from a theoretical innovation to a practical set of clinical tools that can support diagnosis, triage, documentation, workflow coordination, and patient communication when carefully validated, integrated, and monitored. This chapter examines real-world and emerging applications of machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, and generative AI across hospital medicine, radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, nursing, emergency medical services, administrative workflows, and patient portals. Furthermore, we distinguish between AI applications already cleared or deployed in routine clinical settings, applications undergoing prospective or quality-improvement evaluation, and more speculative future use cases. The chapter also addresses critical implementation barriers, including explainability, interoperability, external validation, dataset shift, calibration, fairness across demographic groups, privacy and cybersecurity, hallucination and automation bias in generative AI, and post-deployment monitoring. By evaluating both current deployments and unresolved risks, this chapter outlines a practical “human-in-the-loop” model in which AI serves as a supervised clinical partner rather than a replacement for professional judgment.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The concentration of artificial intelligence (AI) firms may accompany local green patent activity without indicating a greener innovation portfolio or providing useful information about subsequent outcomes. This study evaluates these distinctions using a panel of 295 Chinese cities over 2013–2024. Spatial Durbin estimates combine a positive baseline direct effect of 0.139 with an indirect effect of − 5.901; the latter is sensitive to patent definition and spatial weights. Within-city regressions do not establish a positive green-share association or a difference between green and nongreen patent responses. An expanding-window exercise then predicts outcomes one year ahead using only lagged indicators and benchmarks AI against prior patent performance, total patenting and economic conditions. Across 2020–2024, adding AI reduces the pooled RMSE for green invention applications by 1.43%, with a city-block bootstrap interval of 0.33–2.64%, but increases RMSE for all green applications by 2.95%. The green-share improvement is small and its interval includes zero. These results distinguish spatial association from environmental orientation and forward predictive information. They support an outcome-dependent assessment of AI enterprise counts as an innovation indicator, while providing no evidence of a causal policy effect or a general redirection toward green technologies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Firm Concentration and Urban Green Innovation

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has advanced font generation toward greater diversity, personali-zation, and automation. However, assessing generated fonts remains challenging because quality depends on character identity, glyph structure, style, readability, and aesthetic preference. This structured narrative review synthesizes literature on font generation and quality assessment using four categories: traditional image-quality metrics; character correctness and structural assessment; style, readability, and aesthetic assessment; and multimodal or large-model-based evaluation. The review distinguishes direct typogra-phy-related evidence from methods transferred from general image-quality and multimodal research. Across the literature examined, pixel-level and distribution-level metrics remain useful baselines but cannot alone establish character correctness or typographic suitability. Structure-aware methods and hu-man-centred assessment address complementary dimensions, while vision-language and large-model ap-proaches remain promising but require task-specific validation. The review proposes an integrative gener-ation–evaluation–diagnosis–optimization framework and identifies priorities for transparent benchmarks, interpretable sub-scores, multilingual testing, and reproducible human evaluation.
evidence_items.title: From Generation to Evaluation: A Review of Quality Assessment Methods and Development Trends for Artificial Intelligence-Generated Fonts

evidence_items.summary: Automated neuroimaging meta-analysis is widely used to generate hypotheses and interpret findings, reducing the time and effort required for manual literature searches and evidence curation. However, how closely these methods recover effortful expert-curated syntheses has not been established. We present NeuroMetaBench, an openly available benchmark linking expert curation records across stages of systematic review, from author-stated eligibility criteria and research-article inclusion decisions to individual analysis selections and meta-analysis-specific reference maps. The resource includes bibliographic records for 1,611 research-article inclusions across 17 quantitative review articles and candidate search pools for three. For nine review articles, it also provides analysis-level selections and coordinate data across 35 meta-analyses, documenting which reported results contributed to each meta-analysis and enabling reproducible construction of standardized reference maps. We demonstrate the benchmark's utility by evaluating three established automated methods: Neurosynth, NeuroQuery, and NeuroVLM. Across the benchmark, automated maps generally showed limited to moderate spatial correspondence with expert-curated reference maps, with substantial variation across meta-analysis topics and characteristics. NeuroMetaBench provides an openly available, community-driven resource for evaluating established automated meta-analysis methods, and is well positioned to evaluate emerging LLM-based approaches to automated neuroimaging synthesis.
evidence_items.title: NeuroMetaBench: Expert-curated benchmark for evaluating automated neuroimaging meta-analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Published numerical studies of the telegraph equation differ in their coefficients, boundary data and error measures, so their reported errors seldom allow a direct comparison. This article reviews 22 primary journal publications and compares two time integrators on a shared one-dimensional benchmark. Reanalysis of four published constant-coefficient examples gave observed refinement orders of 0.971–1.041 for first-order schemes and 1.995–1.999 for second-order schemes. The new benchmark uses the same centred spatial stencil with backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule under constant and smoothly varying coefficients. The trapezoidal rule showed approximately second-order convergence in both the spatial and temporal sweeps. Backward Euler approached first order in time on the finest temporal refinements. In the variable-coefficient case, it gave a smaller error on the coarsest jointly refined grid because spatial and temporal errors partly cancelled. At the finest joint resolution, its error was about 7.6 times the trapezoidal error. Both integrators dissipated the discrete energy in unforced tests. Separate refinement sweeps and a common evaluation time make these comparisons more informative than errors reported on a single grid.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Methods for Telegraph Equations: A focused review and a variable coefficient benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present a systematic benchmark of MACE interatomic potentials for iron–nickel alloys, focusing on structural, elastic, and finite-temperature properties of chemically disordered body-centered-cubic (bcc) and face-centered-cubic (fcc) phases. The reference dataset comprises spin-polarized Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof density-functional-theory calculations for special quasirandom structures (SQS) spanning composition, volume, and shear deformation. A system-specific MACE–sqs model trained on this dataset achieves validation errors of 2.0 meV atom − 1 for energies and 24.3 meV Å − 1 for forces. We compare MACE–sqs with several MACE foundation models, including models trained using Hubbard corrections, through equations of state, equilibrium volumes, cubic elastic properties, and thermal lattice expansion. MACE–sqs gives the most consistent overall performance for several zero-temperature structural and elastic benchmarks, although its relative performance depends on property and composition and it does not reproduce all experimental elastic trends. In the finite-temperature comparison, no single model is uniformly superior, and MACE–matpes agrees more closely with experiment for some compositions and comparison metrics. Finite-temperature calculations yield reasonable thermal-expansion coefficients near 300 K, while deviations at elevated temperatures and for magnetovolume sensitive compositions highlight the limitation of representing magnetic effects only implicitly through the spin-polarized reference data. These results define the tested application domain in which targeted SQS-based training improves upon broad foundation models and identify explicit magnetic degrees of freedom and broader configurational sampling as priorities for future development.
evidence_items.title: Capabilities and limitations of MACE interatomic potentials for Fe–Ni alloys: a systematic benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Food-processing expansion does not necessarily translate into greater domestic value capture, particularly in regional production systems that remain strongly dependent on imported intermediate inputs. This study examines food-processing upgrading in Southeast Vietnam as a process of innovative adaptation and reads it against the economic, social and environmental pillars of sustainability. It combines regional evidence on agro-processing development with global value chain (GVC) indicators for the regional manufacturing environment and uses Vietnam's food, beverages and tobacco aggregate (C10T12) as a national sector benchmark. The regional evidence points to improving domestic value capture in agro-processing in Tay Ninh and Binh Phuoc during 2021–2024, within a production structure characterized by high backward participation and predominantly downstream GVC positions. At the national level, two-way fixed-effects estimates for 19 manufacturing sectors over 2018–2022 show that C10T12 increased domestic value-added share and improved GVC position faster than 17 of the 18 other manufacturing sectors. About three-quarters of this gain occurred between 2020 and 2021, the period of most severe pandemic disruption in Southeast Vietnam, and it persisted after reopening. The value-capture gap between primary agriculture and processing narrowed but remained substantial. Set against international agrifood GVC studies, the Vietnamese trajectory is distinctive in combining falling total participation with rising domestic content and a less downstream position. The study contributes an integrative, place-based account in which value capture, chain-wide distribution, adaptive capabilities and production-network position are evaluated jointly.
evidence_items.title: Food Processing and Domestic Value Capture in Southeast Vietnam: Regional Evidence and a National GVC Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Fuel cell hybrid electric vehicle (FCHEV) energy management strategies (EMSs) are commonly evaluated under different vehicle configurations, drive cycles, initial states and modelling assumptions, which complicates direct comparison. This study provides an open-source, reproducible MATLAB/Simulink benchmark for a 50 kW PEMFC and 20 kWh Li-ion battery FCHEV. Nine standard drive cycles are evaluated under fixed vehicle, component, initial-condition and numerical settings using a simple rule-based EMS as the baseline comparator. In the reference simulation, regenerative-braking recovery ranges from 36% on Manhattan to 59% on US06, while fuel-cell conversion losses represent approximately 48%–51% of hydrogen chemical-energy input. Urban cycles spend most of their simulated time at relatively low fuel-cell power, whereas highway operation more frequently occupies the higher-efficiency region. A one-at-a-time and Monte Carlo sensitivity study identifies vehicle mass as the most influential of the investigated parameters on modelled hydrogen consumption. An equivalent consumption minimisation strategy (ECMS) is included only as an illustrative benchmark case, not as a new or state-of-the-art controller. The work does not provide experimental vehicle-level validation; therefore, the numerical results are intended for controlled comparative benchmarking within the defined simulation environment rather than as absolute predictions of a production vehicle. The Simulink model, parameter scripts, selected 1-second outputs and benchmark protocol are documented in the associated repository.
evidence_items.title: A standardised open-source benchmark for cross-cycle evaluation of fuel cell hybrid electric vehicle energy management strategies

evidence_items.summary: This dataset includes the times, positions, and relevant environmental parameters of deep convection initiation (DCI) and Null points used for the analysis documented in the article “The performance of CIN versus CIN depth for anticipating thunderstorm initiation in the central US” published in the American Meteorological Society’s journal Weather and Forecasting .   This dataset is composed of a subset of points in the “Central US deep convection initiation environmental conditions 2008-2015” ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10945611 ) dataset.   The distinguishing characteristics of the current dataset are as follows: Includes environmental parameters using surface-based and mixed-layer parcels and not just most-unstable parcels. evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains finite-volume-based direct numerical simulation (DNS) of single-phase statistically stationary homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) at Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers of 121, resolved on a periodic cubic box with a length of L = 2π m, discretized on a 512^3 grid.   The data are generated using OpenFOAM and stored at a high temporal resolution, covering 1 s of physical time with a writing interval of 0.1 s, which provides a reasonable number of instantaneous flow snapshots for spectral analysis and temporal averaging over a sustained HIT flow. The dataset is accompanied by small, standalone Python scripts for data reading, conversion to CSV format, spectral analysis, and data visualization. Detailed instructions are provided in the accompanying README.md file. This work is part of the ERC-funded project (FragTuRe, grant agreement No. 101160908), and part of this data, as well as the post-processing tools for spectral analysis and enstrophy evolution study, have been used in different publications from this project.
evidence_items.title: DNS data of homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT): spectral analysis with high temporal resolution

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides selected implementation and monitoring data generated under Task 3.2 (T3.2) of Work Package 3 (WP3) of the Horizon Europe MarginUp! project (Grant Agreement No. 101082089). The dataset covers seven use cases across Sweden, Spain, Greece, Germany, Hungary, Argentina and South Africa. It includes use-case characteristics, biomass production and valorisation pathways, selected agronomic and operational performance indicators, farming practices, implementation activities and practical experiences. The dataset draws on Deliverable D3.2 and publicly available Results-Based Monitoring (RBM) data reported in Deliverable D4.3 (Socioeconomic Impact Assessment). The shared RBM framework ensures methodological consistency between WP3 and WP4. While the WP4 dataset focuses on socioeconomic assessment, this dataset specifically addresses practical implementation, agronomic performance and operational monitoring of biomass production and valorisation pathways on marginal lands. The dataset contains selected, processed and generalised research data. Commercially sensitive information, detailed financial data, confidential technical specifications and personal information are excluded. Access to additional underlying data is subject to applicable confidentiality, intellectual property and data-sharing arrangements. For further information, please contact the MarginUp! project coordination team at marginup@atb-potsdam.de .
evidence_items.title: MarginUp! Use-case Implementation and Monitoring Dataset

It gives the timeline (tool configurations frozen before any measurement), the research questions, the primary criterion (does the matching rule between expected and recovered files change the ranking of the tools?), the secondary analyses (complementarity of file-system metadata and carving, per-scenario results, precision and written volume, default versus expert configurations) and the rules for failures and time-outs. The archive contains: the preregistration and its deviation log; the pilot results declared as predictions; the evaluation specification (v1.2); the reference implementation of overlap-based matching (optimal one-to-one assignment, coverage, purity, order, decodability), the image-level inference and their tests; the image forgers; the default and expert configurations of PhotoRec 7.2, Foremost 1.5.7, Scalpel 1.60, tsk recover 4.12.1 and 4.15.0 and Scalpel3 3.53.0 with pinned packages; the replay of NIST CFTT reports; and the ground truth of the 40 images (SHA-256 of each image, byte-level layout of each placed file). Documents in English (reference version); code and code comments in French, with a glossary.

evidence_items.summary: This research data and reproducibility package supports the manuscript “Beyond a Coastal Corridor: Early Occupations and Ecological Complementarity in Tacna and the South-Central Andes” (Version B27). The dataset comprises 117 published radiocarbon records, including 46 core determinations and 71 regional comparative records, 92 marginal posterior distributions calibrated using SHCal20, Bayesian chronological comparisons, supplementary sensitivity analyses, archaeological statistics, generalized geospatial data, scientific figures, Excel workbooks, and executable Python code. Computational verification reproduced all 276 marginal quantiles, 20 core probability checks, and six regional comparisons under the documented analytical assumptions. The archive provides a transparent and reproducible framework for investigating early human occupations, ecological complementarity, and potential mobility corridors in the South-Central Andes. The research is based on secondary analysis of published archaeological evidence. Computational reproducibility does not constitute independent laboratory validation or demonstrate specific migration routes. The archive includes source registers, methodological limitations, data dictionaries, and integrity checks.
evidence_items.title: Beyond a Coastal Corridor: Early Occupations and Ecological Complementarity in Tacna and the South-Central Andes — Research Data and Reproducibility Package

evidence_items.summary: Morphing Attack Detection (MAD) systems often suffer from performance degradation when deployed in operational environments, such as airports, that differ from the training domain. We propose an adaptive differential MAD framework that continuously refines a pre-trained detector using live bona fide samples acquired at the gate. The system is memoryless, so no samples are stored in memory to mitigate privacy concerns about the collection of personal data. To prevent the loss of discriminative power caused by bona fide-only adaptation, the method generates synthetic morph samples on-the-fly by combining the current operational subject with identities from an external public or synthetic face dataset. The adaptation process further relies on a quality-aware bona fide selection strategy and a controlled balancing mechanism for synthetic morph generation. Experimental results show that the proposed method improves target-domain specialization while maintaining robustness against morph attacks.
evidence_items.title: Quality-driven Adaptive Morphing Attack Detection in Operational Scenarios via Online Learning

evidence_items.summary: The paper studies overreliance on AI. It asks whether advice from three AI models built by different developers, rather than one, reduces how often people adopt a wrong AI answer, and whether this depends on the models making the same errors. Seeing three models reduced the adoption of wrong answers, but only when the models' errors diverged. A wrong answer repeated by a second model was adopted as often as a single model's wrong answer. This archive holds the analysis code, study materials, aggregate data and a simulated dataset for Studies 1–2 (N = 441) of 'Advice from multiple AI models reduces overreliance only when their errors diverge'. Individual-level data are not included: under the consent participants gave, they cannot be shared publicly but are available to qualified researchers on request. Code is released under the MIT License; data, materials and documentation under CC BY 4.0, except MMLU-Pro content (Apache 2.0).
evidence_items.title: Data and code for: Advice from multiple AI models reduces overreliance only when their errors diverge

evidence_items.summary: Early identification of at-risk students enables timely pedagogical support, yet new courses and small cohorts often lack labelled history for supervised learning, early grades are sparse, and activity drops sharply during holidays. We present a training-free methodology in the xAPIens platform that maps learning events into a risk index traceable to three pedagogical dimensions: academic performance, cohort-relative engagement, and calendar study rhythm. Rather than competing with supervised models on large historical archives, we test three practical cold-start questions: whether ranking holds without retuning, whether the pipeline prevents alert collapse under missing grades and real holidays, and whether profiles separate meaningful risk patterns. With frozen parameters across all four OULAD offerings (22 course offerings), the pipeline achieves mean AP 0.64–0.79 (6.4–8.4 at-risk students per 10 contacted against 3.6–4.9/10 base rates) and higher AP than simple activity counts in most courses from week 3 onward (by 0.03–0.07 on average). Skipping absent grades (NO DATA) reduces week-2 critical false alarms (R ≥ 0.80) among passing students from 88.1% to 12.4%. During the real Christmas breaks in OULAD (2014J −70%, 2013J −56%), cohort normalization reduces the alert surge among active students over 3.5-fold (+6.3 vs. +21.8 pp in 2014J; +3.6 vs. +13.0 pp in 2013J), whereas across all enrolled students (over half inactive during the break) the gap is modest (+16.7 vs. +23.3 pp), indicating that holiday-week alerts should not be acted upon directly. A gender parity check in OULAD at the top-25% cutoff reveals a residual recall gap for at-risk women even within courses (37.4% vs. 44.8% macro-averaged), reinforcing the need for human oversight. Four weekly chronologies from OULAD illustrate profile behavior, including a false-alarm case; live xAPI validation and direct evaluation with instructors remain future work.
evidence_items.title: Robust and Traceable Early Academic Risk Detection Without Historical Data in the xAPIens Platform

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This paper develops a variational-analytic and information-theoretic framework for investigating Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) partial products Π {p ≤ X} (N p / p) and Hasse–Weil Euler products L(E, s) for elliptic curves E over the rational numbers ℚ . Building upon our previously established formalism of identical local Chebyshev error cancellation and two-stage entropy cascades for the sum-of-divisors function, we transfer the logarithmic regularization method from the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) to elliptic curve L-series. We prove an unconditional theorem on the mutual cancellation of leading local fluctuations between the logarithmic point-count product N p = #E( 𝔽 p) and the cumulative Frobenius trace sum ∑ {p ≤ X} a p / p (Lemma 1), and we isolate a deterministic quadratic stabilization buffer generated by squared Frobenius traces a p² / (2p²) and higher prime powers (Theorem 1). Within the thermodynamic free-energy and Legendre transform formalism, we formulate a dimensionless elliptic duality invariant I E(X) linking rational point density saturation to prime-free primorial vacuum gaps, and determine critical convergence thresholds for curves of algebraic rank r = 0, 1, 2 on a logarithmic grid. Computational verification on benchmark Cremona curves 11a1 (r = 0), 37a1 (r = 1), and 389a1 (r = 2) confirms the suppression of local Sato–Tate dispersion noise and monotonic convergence of the logarithmic profile toward the asymptotic law r · ln(ln X) + ln C E.
evidence_items.title: Local Error Cancellation and Entropy-Cascade Bounds in Hasse–Weil  Euler Products for Elliptic Curves

evidence_items.summary: The first half-value layer (HVL), defined as the thickness of material required to reduce the x-ray beam intensity (air kerma) to 50%, is a key radiation quality specifier. Although HVL has been measured for decades using ionization chambers and aluminum filters, the detailed measurement procedures and associated uncertainties remain insufficiently established. With the growing use of x-ray multimeters (XMMs) capable of measuring HVL directly from the x-ray beam, reliable calibration and uncertainty evaluation are needed. This work presents a detailed approach for determining the first HVL and calibrating XMMs for RQR 2, RQR 5, and RQR 10 standard radiation qualities for radiography as defined in IEC 61 267. The uncertainty budget is structured into three steps: measured HVL, reference HVL, and HVL calibration coefficient, emphasizing the effects of ionization chamber energy dependence and field size. The reference HVLs for RQR 2, RQR 5, and RQR 10 were 1.417 mm Al, 2.570 mm Al, and 6.510 mm Al, respectively, with expanded uncertainties ( k = 2) of 1.0%, 1.1%, and 1.7%. The corresponding HVL calibration coefficients had uncertainties of 1.4%, 1.3%, and 1.8%.
evidence_items.title: Calibration of X-ray multimeters for half-value layer: measurement methods and uncertainty evaluation

evidence_items.summary: The use of wireless sensor networks (WSN) for monitoring physical and chemical variables in large areas allows density and frequency measurements which have been unavailable to date in classical measurement systems. To fully take advantage of this technology in a particular application, besides an accurate design and selection of all the components involved in its operation, it is essential to dispose of reliable lifetime estimation prior to deployment. This paper presents an experimental approach to determine the actual lifetime of such battery-operated systems, making use of a customWSNarchitecture, and for different batteries technologies. To render a reliable evaluation, the energy consumption of the sensor nodes under their different operation modes, in correlation with the battery characteristics and the voltage regulation system, is jointly considered. The result is a complete and practical lifetime model, whose appropriate performance has been validated in a real deployment scenario.
evidence_items.title: Reliable Lifespan Evaluation of a Remote Environment Monitoring System Based on Wireless Sensor Networks and Global System for Mobile Communications

evidence_items.summary: This article presents a structured narrative review of publicly available research on radar development, small-object sensing challenges, and lessons reported in local and regional conflicts. The study compares historical stages of radar development, identifies recurrent research themes, and discusses the limitations of interpreting conflict observations as universal technical evidence. Results are presented as a qualitative synthesis rather than experimental performance claims. Particular attention is given to publications by Uzbekistan-based researchers alongside international peer-reviewed and institutional sources. The analysis concludes that radar evolution is best understood as an interaction among sensor science, information management, institutional learning, and responsible evaluation, rather than as a single technological breakthrough.
evidence_items.title: THE EVOLUTION OF RADAR SYSTEMS AMID THE WIDESPREAD USE OF UNMANNED AERIAL VEHICLES: LESSONS FROM LOCAL CONFLICTS

evidence_items.summary: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $Σ= (Σ O, Σ A, Σ R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $Σ O / Σ A / Σ R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $Σ O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $Σ A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io
evidence_items.title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management

evidence_items.summary: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at https://github.com/alanzhangcs/MonoPCA.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation

evidence_items.summary: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.
evidence_items.title: GRAPE-Bench: When Vision Degrades, Does Video Reasoning Hold?

evidence_items.summary: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with π_{0.5} and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
evidence_items.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies

evidence_items.summary: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.
evidence_items.title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.
evidence_items.title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Optimization benchmarks play a fundamental role in assessing algorithm performance; however, existing artificial benchmarks often fail to capture the diversity and irregularity of real-world problem structures, while benchmarks derived from real-world problems are costly and difficult to construct. To address these challenges, we propose an evolutionary automatic benchmark generation framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) as a generative operator, termed the LLM-driven evolutionary benchmark generator (LLM-EBG). In this framework, the LLM serves as an evolutionary operator that generates and evolves benchmark problems within a flexible, expressive representation space. As a case study, we generate unconstrained single-objective continuous minimization problems represented as mathematical expressions designed to induce significant performance differences between a genetic algorithm (GA) and differential evolution (DE). Experimental results show that LLM-EBG successfully produces benchmark problems in which the designated target algorithm consistently outperforms the comparative algorithm in more than 80% of trials. Furthermore, exploratory landscape analysis reveals that benchmarks favoring GA are highly sensitive to variable scaling, demonstrating that the proposed framework can generate problems with distinct geometric characteristics that reflect the intrinsic search behaviors of different optimization algorithms.
evidence_items.title: An evolutionary framework for automatic optimization benchmark generation via large language models

evidence_items.summary: We propose an efficient content detection method generated by large language models (LLMs), referred to as Mahalanobis distance–based confidence score (MDCS)–based detection (MDCSD), that fully harnesses the universality of LLMs across multiple splits. Its essence lies in utilizing the MDCS of the text as the ultimate discriminative feature. The prerequisite for computing the MDCS is the efficient joint estimation of the precision matrices corresponding to multiple splits. We provide regularization techniques for constructing the joint estimator and offer corresponding computationally feasible optimization algorithms. The sparsity and consistency of the joint estimator are demonstrated. Based on offset Rademacher complexity, we further derive the optimal excess risk bound for the detection problem. Superiority of MDCSD is validated on the recently released Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus data set. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science and Machine Learning. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants W2511079, 72471010, 72250065, and 72325007], the Xiangjiang Laboratory Key Project [Grant 23XJ02004], and the Science and Technology Innovation Program of Hunan Province [Grant 2024RC7003]. Supplemental Material: The software that supports the findings of this study is available within the paper and its Supplemental Information ( https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/suppl/10.1287/ijoc.2024.0877 ) as well as from the IJOC GitHub software repository ( https://github.com/INFORMSJoC/2024.0877 ). The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

evidence_items.summary: Background: The physician global assessment (PhGA) is a core outcome measure in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) but is incompletely captured, even in clinical registries. We developed a large language model (LLM) approach that extracts explicitly documented PhGA from clinical narratives and infers a score where none is recorded. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address both tasks. Methods: We linked charts from 306 children with JIA at one center to the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry (2016-2024). A structured prompt was developed on 100 randomly sampled charts, then evaluated on 400 charts from patients not represented in the development set. Extraction used GPT-5.2 within a HIPAA-compliant Azure environment. Registry-recorded PhGA served as the reference standard, with discordances adjudicated by a pediatric rheumatologist blinded to both sources. Agreement was assessed by intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(2,1)), exact match, and mean absolute error (MAE). Results: Against registry values, ICC(2,1) was 0.87 (95% CI 0.85-0.89; n=400), with 70.5% exact agreement and MAE 0.363. Agreement was near-perfect for explicit extractions (n=190; ICC 0.99; 95% CI 0.98-0.99) and lower for inferred scores (n=210; ICC 0.72; 95% CI 0.64-0.78). Large discordances (≥2 points) occurred in 7.3% of cases. Against the adjudicated standard, overall ICC(2,1) was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97), with 77.5% exact agreement and MAE 0.200. All 14 explicit discordances reflected mismatch between the registry and the clinical note, rather than extraction errors (adjudicated ICC 1.00). For inferred scores, ICC rose to 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.92). Residual disagreement was concentrated at the inactive/minimally active boundary. Conclusion: An LLM can reliably extract PhGA from clinical notes with high accuracy to support downstream clinical research, offering a scalable approach to mitigating missingness in patient registries.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Extraction and Inference of Physician Global Assessment from Clinical Notes in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

evidence_items.summary: Smart public spaces combine sensing infrastructures, digital services, responsive facilities, and physical spatial elements, producing experience evidence that cannot be adequately represented by questionnaires or isolated environmental indicators. This study develops a multimodal artificial intelligence model that evaluates comfort, perceived safety, spatial engagement, accessibility, and an integrated experience score from synchronized behavioral video, UWB trajectories, environmental sensing, and textual feedback. Data are collected from 120 participants completing four eight-minute spatial conditions in an instrumented campus plaza. Modality-specific encoders generate 128-dimensional representations, which are temporally aligned and integrated by a four-layer cross-modal Transformer with hierarchical regression heads. On participant-independent testing, the proposed model achieved an overall MAE of 0.044 ± 0.004, RMSE of 0.061 ± 0.005, R² of 0.905 ± 0.012, and Spearman ρ of 0.951 ± 0.008, significantly outperforming early-fusion and single-modality baselines (p < .001). Removing trajectory or textual information increased overall MAE to 0.061 ± 0.006 and 0.059 ± 0.005, respectively. The model also retained stable performance across crowd-density and lighting conditions, while SHAP analysis identified distinct modality contributions to each experience dimension.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Based Evaluation Model for Smart Public Space Experience

evidence_items.summary: The comprehensive evaluation of college physical education teaching effects is critical for ensuring both student performance and instructional quality. This study proposes the AI-IoT Physical Performance Fusion System (AIPPF), which integrates multimodal wearable sensor data, vision-based pose estimation, and a CNN-Transformer fusion model for automated performance scoring. The system synchronizes physiological signals with biomechanical movement analysis to deliver real-time monitoring, movement error detection, personalized feedback, and scalable institutional integration. Experimental findings demonstrate that AIPPF achieves over 90% accuracy in evaluation compared to 65–85% for traditional and fuzzy evaluation models, reduces safety risks to 6–16% versus 30–40% in prior methods, lowers fatigue accumulation by 15–20%, and enhances student engagement scores to above 85%, reaching a maximum of 94% in gamified sessions. Computation efficiency was also improved, with response times of 35–50 ms, enabling real-time classroom application.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of College Physical Education Teaching Effects Based on Artificial Intelligence and IoT

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To evaluate ambient Artificial Intelligence (AI) scribe systems (AAS) across multiple domains using a rapid learning health system (LHS) approach, including provider satisfaction, efficiency, documentation quality, usability, and patient sentiment. Materials and Methods This LHS evaluation compared 2 AAS systems (Abridge and Nabla) among 100 providers over 90 days. Evaluation incorporated a cluster randomized crossover comparison, analysis of use and EHR-based workflow outcomes, and standardized simulated encounters to assess documentation quality and safety. Outcomes included provider satisfaction, efficiency, note quality, usability, and patient sentiment. Results In standardized simulated encounters, both systems achieved 76% note element accuracy with minimal risk for harm. In the randomized crossover comparison, Abridge demonstrated higher usability scores (78.5 vs 73) and was preferred 3:1 over Nabla, which had higher automated speech recognition error rates. Across 16 479 clinical encounters, AAS was used in 35.7% of visits. Total EHR time decreased by approximately 5 minutes per day; same-day chart closure increased by approximately 5% during the initial crossover period, but this effect was attenuated. Provider experience was positive (Net Promoter Score [NPS] 53). Discussion Both systems demonstrated comparable documentation accuracy and modest efficiency gains while improving clinician satisfaction. Despite similar performance, clinicians reported differences in usability and preference. Adoption below 40% reflected the trade-off between documentation support and verification burden. Conclusion Rapid, multidimensional evaluation within a LHS can assess AAS across domains of implementation, efficiency, clinician experience, and documentation quality and safety. Ongoing monitoring of efficiency, documentation quality, and use patterns is essential.
evidence_items.title: Rapid comparative evaluation of 2 ambient artificial intelligence applications in a learning health system

evidence_items.summary: Natural products (NPs) remain a valuable source of chemical diversity for pharmacological research and drug development. Their complex structures and biological activities have contributed to the discovery of medicines and inspired new therapeutic strategies. Nevertheless, conventional natural-product discovery can be slow and resource-intensive because researchers must address source selection, extraction, isolation, dereplication, structural elucidation, biological testing and subsequent optimization. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), natural-language processing, computer vision and graph-based methods, offers computational approaches to help manage these tasks. This review discusses the role of AI across the natural-product discovery pipeline, with emphasis on data integration, plant and microbial source exploration, biosynthetic gene-cluster analysis, metabolomics and spectral interpretation, activity and target prediction, virtual screening, network pharmacology, toxicity and ADMET estimation, and molecular design. It also describes commonly used databases and computational resources, outlines a practical AI-supported workflow, and considers opportunities for integrating experimental evidence with computational predictions. The benefits of AI include prioritization of candidate compounds, improved analysis of large and heterogeneous datasets, hypothesis generation and more systematic exploration of chemical and biological relationships. Important limitations remain, including dataset bias, inconsistent annotation, small sample sizes, overfitting, poor external validation, limited interpretability, reproducibility concerns and the need for experimental confirmation. Ethical, regulatory and biodiversity considerations are also discussed. AI is best regarded as a decision-support layer that complementsnot replacesphytochemistry, pharmacology, analytical chemistry and biological experimentation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Natural Products Discovery

evidence_items.summary: AI transforms financial reporting via predictive anomaly detection, semantic analysis, and continuous auditing. The fractured literature between computer science and accounting lacks a unified framework. To correct this, a scoping review mapped global scholarship. Evaluating 562 Scopus records published before April 2026 exposed exponential growth between 2020 and 2025. Reflexive Thematic Analysis yielded four themes: algorithmic classification predicting distress; semantic quantification decoding narratives; continuous audits using robotic workflows; and ethical hurdles from transparency barriers. Bridging this gap demands grounding machine learning in accounting theories. Future operations must implement explainable AI, align with sustainable development goals, and obey regulatory standards.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Reporting Systems

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: Skin cancers represent some of the most common cancers worldwide. Its incidence is constantly rising. Early detection is essential to reduce morbidity and improve survival. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI)-based software has increasingly been integrated into 2D/3D total-body-photography (TBP) systems, to support clinicians in diagnosing cutaneous lesions. Objectives: To evaluate VIDIX 4.0 diagnostic performance using histopathology as the reference standard and assess the ability of the DEXI score to discriminate between malignant and benign lesions. Methods: This monocenter retrospective study included 204 lesions from 165 patients who underwent VIDIX 4.0 videodermoscopy, followed by excision and histopathological examination. Diagnostic performance was evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy, with 95% confidence intervals calculated using the Wilson method. Malignant and benign lesions were compared after excluding actinic keratoses. DEXI scores were analyzed using Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney U tests with Holm adjustment. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed DEXI discrimination using the area under the curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals. Results: VIDIX sensitivity was 93.3% for nevi, 81.8% for basal cell carcinoma (BCC), 63.2% for melanoma, 44.4% for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), 33.3% for actinic keratosis (AK), and 61.1% for seborrheic keratosis (SK). For malignant versus benign lesions, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 80.3%, 92.7%, and 88.9%, respectively. DEXI scores differed significantly among histopathological categories (P<0.0001), showing good discrimination between malignant and benign lesions (AUC, 0.939; 95% CI, 0.896–0.974).
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Videodermoscopy System for Cutaneous Lesion Classification: A Retrospective Study

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) holds great promise in radiotherapy. However, prospective evaluation and robust assessment frameworks for AI contouring and planning tools are lacking, casting doubt on the quality and cost-effectiveness of some AI radiotherapy solutions and hindering wider clinical deployment. ARCHERY, an international, prospective multi-cancer basket trial, seeks to undertake a large-scale evaluation of AI-assisted contouring and planning for cancers of the head and neck, prostate and cervix for patients in diverse country settings. We describe the evaluation approach led by the UK Radiotherapy Trials Quality Assurance (RTTQA) Group which, through literature appraisal, established protocol-defined reference standard contour and planning parameters and, following a scoping review and consensus discussion, developed evaluation definitions to enable robust and consistent assessment. This approach demonstrates a strong example of AI radiotherapy study methodology and tool assessment, and serves as a foundation for adoption, adaptation and development in future AI radiotherapy studies.
evidence_items.title: Defining an evaluation framework for radiotherapy trials which use artificial intelligence- lessons from the ARCHERY trial

evidence_items.summary: This chapter examines how immersive technologies and artificial intelligence can enhance accessible tourism experiences for people with disabilities. Building on literature on tourism constraints and the tourism value chain, it first discusses physical, informational, communicative, cognitive, attitudinal, and psychological barriers that shape travel participation. It then evaluates the accessibility roles of virtual reality, augmented reality, extended reality, metaverse environments, robot-supported systems, and AI-based smart tourism platforms across pre-travel planning, on-site experience, remote participation, and post-travel feedback. The chapter argues that these technologies can support destination preview, real-time guidance, multimodal communication, personalization, remote access, and service improvement. However, it also emphasizes that technology should complement, not replace, accessible infrastructure, trained personnel, ethical data governance, and participatory design involving people with disabilities.
evidence_items.title: Immersive Technologies and Artificial Intelligence for Accessible Tourism

evidence_items.summary: This chapter explores how artificial intelligence reshapes assessment design in higher education, using Cantonese as a second language as a distinctive lens. Cantonese's tonal and sociolinguistic complexity provides a rigorous case for evaluating AI's role in oral proficiency testing. The discussion highlights the shift toward adaptive, learner-centred formats that move beyond standardised methods. Drawing on Hong Kong's higher education practices, it demonstrates how integrating Automatic Speech Recognition, Large Language Models, and Text-to-Speech enables contextualized tasks, real-time feedback, and alignment with ACTFL and CEFR frameworks. It also addresses challenges of transparency, cultural sensitivity, and human-in-the-loop mediation. Ultimately, AI-driven assessment design fosters flexible, inclusive, and pedagogically robust approaches across multilingual higher education.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Assessment Design for Cantonese Education

evidence_items.summary: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is the most common chronic inflammatory skin disease in high-income countries and is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity and a relapsing course. Despite its high prevalence, the diagnosis of AD remains largely clinical and is often challenging due to overlapping features with other inflammatory dermatoses, the absence of definitive biomarkers, and variability in disease presentation across age groups and skin types. These challenges may lead to diagnostic delay or misclassification, with potential implications for disease management and patient outcomes. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning and deep learning approaches, has emerged as a promising tool in dermatology. AI-based systems have demonstrated encouraging performance in diagnosing various skin diseases using clinical photographs, advanced imaging, molecular and laboratory approaches, and have increasingly been applied to AD, achieving high sensitivity and specificity in several studies. Such tools may support clinicians by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, assisting in differential diagnosis, and serving as effective screening instruments, especially in primary care or resource-limited settings. Importantly, AI is intended to complement rather than replace clinical expertise. This review summarizes the current literature on AI applications in the diagnosis of AD, critically evaluates existing models, and discusses their readiness for clinical translation, while highlighting key gaps that must be addressed to bridge research and routine clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis of Atopic Dermatitis
